Re:
Pesticide Registration Review; Proposed Interim Decision for Carbaryl; Docket 
Identification Number EPA-HQ-OPP-2010-0230
Dear Dr. Reaves:
The California Citrus Quality Council (CCQC) and California Citrus Mutual (CCM) represent
approximately 1,500 citrus growers and 80 packinghouses in California, whose total farmgate 
value of California citrus production including oranges, lemons, mandarins and grapefruit in the 
2021-22 marketing year was $2.3 billion.  The industry employs over 21,000 people on a full-
time basis.  We appreciate this opportunity to comment on the proposed interim decision (PID) 
for carbaryl.
While the use of carbaryl in the California citrus industry is limited, it is an important pesticide 
in some specific circumstances.  The primary use is to control California red scale when other 
pesticides have not provided adequate control.  It is also used in California red scale eradication 
programs in southern California.
Many pest control advisors and growers avoid the use of carbaryl because it is a broad spectrum 
pesticide that has the potential to impact beneficial insects that most growers try to nurture as 
part of their biologically based integrated pest management (IPM) programs.  However, 
California red scale is a serious economic pest in California citrus production.  High populations 
of the pest reduce tree vigor, fruit size and yield.  It is also a quarantine pest the industry’s most 
important export market valued at $226 million annually.  Citrus shipments containing the pest 
are subject to rejection by the importing country.

Page 2
When California red scale populations are high, many available pesticide alternatives will not 
effectively control it.  Consequently, its presence can persist even when growers are doing their 
best to control it.  Most recently, average annual temperatures in California have increased in 
consecutive years which has provided insects, including California red scale, longer seasonal 
growth potential leading to higher populations.  Carbaryl is a tool that some citrus growers are 
using to effectively manage California red scale in situations where it is particularly hard to 
address with available alternatives.  It is also used in place of chlorpyrifos, which was recently 
cancelled, in a California red scale eradication program in southern California.
The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (the Agency) is proposing to reduce the single use 
carbaryl maximum rate to 5 lbs. of active ingredient per acre as part of its PID.  This rate is too 
low to effectively control California red scale in citrus.  This rate effectively eliminates the use 
of carbaryl in California citrus production.  Growers who are using carbaryl for California red 
scale, primarily use rates averaging between five and twelve pounds of active ingredient per acre.
CCQC does not object to EPA’s proposal to require additional personal protective equipment 
(PPE) to address potential mixer / loader exposures.  However, CCQC does not agree that EPA 
has accurately assessed the ecological risk posed by carbaryl use in California citrus production.  
While the Agency outlines the LD 50 properties of carbaryl and the potential impact on various 
species, it does not demonstrate how the current minimal use of carbaryl would lead to exposures 
that would necessitate a 58 percent reduction in the maximum single use rate.  It appears that 
EPA’s assessment is a theoretical estimate of the potential ecological risk using a set of worst-
case estimates.
The California Department of Pesticide Regulation (CDPR) is a reliable source of pesticide 
usage data in California, and the data demonstrate there is minimal use of carbaryl on citrus.  It is 
highly unlikely that the amount of carbaryl being used on citrus would result in any significant 
ecological risk if actual usage data were used to assess the risk.  Additionally, the majority of the 
use of carbaryl would be in the summer months, during a period where there is very little, if any, 
rainfall where carbaryl is used.  Under these conditions, it isn’t likely that carbaryl use on citrus 
would threaten any aquatic species.  Given these considerations and the critical importance of 
carbaryl to California citrus growers, CCQC and CCM are requesting that EPA reconsider its 
methodology.
Specifically, CCQC and CCM are requesting that EPA reconsider the 5 lb. active ingredient per 
acre restriction.  California citrus growers could still utilize carbaryl if a rate of 8 lbs. of active 
ingredient per acre were permitted along with a 300 foot buffer from salmon habitats.  
Considering the limited use of carbaryl, a rate reduction to 8 lbs., the Agency’s proposed 
additional personal protective equipment requirement and the benefits this use provides 
California citrus growers, we believe EPA could revise its proposed decision to adequately 
address risks of concern associated with the use carbaryl on California citrus.
CCQC and CCM noted the Agency’s concerns about pollinator risks from carbaryl use in its 
PID.  The State of California has established extensive protections to bees during citrus bloom 
periods including a prohibition on the use of carbaryl from the beginning of bloom until pedal 
fall. We believe the current state protections are sufficiently protective of pollinators to address 
the Agency’s concerns.

Page 3
Finally, we are seeking clarification of the language used on page 45 of the PID.  The PID states 
the following:
“Require double layer, gloves, chemical resistant headgear, and PF10 respirator for 
broadcast airblast applications up to 3 lbs ai/A” (emphasis added)
Other than in the above-quoted language, throughout the PID, the Agency explicitly states that it 
is limiting the single maximum rate on citrus to 5 lbs. of active ingredient per acre.  The Agency 
offers no explanation or rational to support restricting the application rate on citrus to 3 lb. active 
ingredient.  However, the 3 lb. active ingredient maximum rate would amount to a cancellation 
of the citrus use in California since the rate would be ineffective for California red scale.  
We appreciate this opportunity to comment on this important matter.
Sincerely yours,
                                                       
James R. Cranney, Jr., President                                              Casey Creamer, President/CEO
California Citrus Quality Council                                            California Citrus Mutual

Dear Ms. Romanovsky: 
On behalf of the California Stormwater Quality Association (CASQA),1 thank you for this opportunity to comment on 
the Proposed Interim Registration Review Decision (“PID”) 2 for carbaryl. CASQA also reviewed EPA’s recently 
released Draft Evaluation Supporting Proposed Mitigations Predicted to Avoid Jeopardy and Adverse Modification of 
Designated Critical Habitat and Reduce Take for Four Federally Listed Endangered and Threatened Species (“BE 
Memo”).3 
 
As noted in the Draft Ecological Risk Assessment (ERA), 4 carbaryl is registered for outdoor use as a carbamate 
insecticide and plant growth regulator with both agricultural and non-agricultural uses. While EPA’s pesticide 
registration review process proceeds pursuant to the Federal Insecticide, Fungicide, and Rodenticide Act (FIFRA), 
there is an important nexus with the requirements of the federal Clean Water Act (CWA), which regulates urban 
runoff discharges to waters of the United States (commonly known as “receiving waters”) through the National 
Pollutant Discharge Elimination System (NPDES) permit program.  
 
The results of EPA’s registration review for carbaryl have important implications for our members’ CWA compliance, 
as local agencies are held responsible for the quality of urban runoff discharges conveyed to receiving waters 
through municipal storm drainage systems. When pesticide-related water pollution occurs, municipalities can be 
subject to CWA enforcement actions under the terms of their NPDES permits. Municipalities also face negative 
publicity and potential litigation under the citizen suit provisions of the CWA.5   
 
1 CASQA is a nonprofit corporation that advances sustainable stormwater management protective of California water resources.  With 
approximately 2,000 members, our membership is comprised of a diverse range of stormwater quality management organizations and 
individuals, including over 180 cities, 23 counties, special districts, federal agencies, state agencies, ports, universities and school districts, 
wastewater agencies, water suppliers, industries, and consulting firms throughout the state.  Collectively, CASQA represents over 26 million 
people in California.

COMMENT #1:  CASQA SUPPORTS EPA’S PROPOSED MITIGATION MEASURES FOR CARBARYL 
Given the high degree of threat posed by carbaryl use in the urban environment, as thoroughly documented in the 
Draft ERA and PID, CASQA supports the inclusion of the following proposed mitigation measures as enumerated in 
the PID: 
Use Deletions: the prohibition of residential dust formulations and residential granule formations for use on turf 
(because these are often applied incorrectly and end up on impervious surfaces such as sidewalks) 
Spray Drift Management measures, including limits on wind speed and inclusion of buffer zones for aquatic 
habitats. As specified in Appendix B [PID p. 84] this includes “Buffer Zones to Water Bodies for residential 
applications”, with the following statement required in the label’s Directions for Use:  
“Do not apply within 25 feet of aquatic habitats (such as, but not limited to, lakes, reservoirs, rivers, streams, 
marshes, ponds, estuaries, and commercial fish ponds).” 
General Environmental Protection Measures, including mitigation measures for outdoor urban uses in 
residential and commercial settings (i.e., structural, turf, ornamental, nursery) to reduce the amount of carbaryl in 
the urban environment that enters outdoor drainage systems and waterbodies, and mitigate potential risks to 
aquatic organisms. These proposed measures include improved label language for carbaryl product labels, to be 
included within the Directions for Use, specifically:  
• 
Statements for Outdoor Label Consistency [PID pp. 54-55. App. B p. 85-86]: label changes to ensure 
consistency among various products and with current EPA policy. This includes label language to state 
maximum application rates and define the maximum size of a treatment that may be considered a spot 
treatment:  
“Spot treatments must not exceed two square feet in size”  
• 
General Outdoor Application Statements [PID p. 55, App. B p. 84]: “All outdoor spray applications must be 
limited to spot or crack-and-crevice treatments only, except for the following permitted uses: 
1. Applications to soil, lawn, turf, or vegetation; 
2. Perimeter band treatments of 6 ft wide or less from the base of a man-made structure to pervious 
surfaces (e.g., soil, mulch, or lawn); 
3. Applications around potential exterior pest entry points into man-made structures such as doorways 
and windows, when limited to a band not to exceed one inch; 
4. Applications to vertical surfaces directly above pervious surfaces, such as bare soil, lawn, turf, mulch or 
other vegetation, that do not drain into ditches, storm drains, gutters, or surface waters.” 
The proposed improved product label language also includes measures intended to reduce the amount of runoff 
entering waterbodies and drainage systems, specifically: 
• 
Water Protection Statements [PID p. 55-56, App. B p. 85]: 
o “Do not spray the product into fish pools, ponds, streams, or lakes. Do not apply directly to sewers 
or drains, or to any area like a gutter where drainage to sewers, storm drains, water bodies, or 
aquatic habitat can occur.” 
o “Do not allow the product to enter any drain during or after application.” 
o “Do not apply directly to impervious horizontal surfaces such as sidewalks, driveways, and patios 
except as a spot or crack-and-crevice treatment.” 
o “Do not apply to vertical surfaces directly above pervious or impervious surfaces that drain into 
ditches, storm drains, gutters, or surface waters.” 
o “Do not apply or irrigate to the point of run-off.”

• 
Rain-Related Statements [PID p. 56, App. B p. 85]: 
o “Do not apply carbaryl containing products during rain.” 
o “Do not apply carbaryl containing products when a storm event likely to produce runoff from the 
treated area is forecasted (by NOAA/National Weather Service, or other similar forecasting service) 
to occur within 48 hours following application.” 
o “Do not apply carbaryl products when soils are saturated or above field capacity.” 
• 
Statements for Crack-and-Crevice Treatments [PID p. 56, App. B p. 90]: 
o “Treat exposed surfaces to cover thoroughly but avoid excess run-off.” 
o “To treat insects harbored in voids and cracks-and-crevices, applications must be made in such a 
manner to limit dripping and avoid runoff onto untreated structural surfaces and plants.” 
CASQA further supports the additional mitigations proposed to reduce drift and runoff from non-broadcast/non-
agricultural applications pursuant to implementing the NMFS Salmonid Biological Opinion [PID pp. 64-65, App. G 
pp. 110-111], including specifically the following label statements designed to reduce drift and runoff from 
urban/residential environments. Those statements reflect the mitigations proposed for non-listed species in the 
Memo [App. B, pp. 80-83], and they generally reiterate the mitigations included in the proposed label language 
as cited above, with the addition of the incident reporting language: 
o Reporting Ecological Incidents: To report ecological incidents, including mortality, injury, or harm to 
plants and animals, call [insert registrant phone number]. 
CASQA also supports the inclusion of updated Environmental Hazard Statements on carbaryl product labels 
[PID App. B, pp. 79-80]. Although residential, non-professional use of carbaryl has been banned in California 
since 2020, CASQA remains concerned about residential products due the prevalence of online purchases of 
pesticides, which can also include out-of-state purchase of residential products that include carbaryl. To this end, 
CASQA supports the proposed inclusion of the carbaryl product labels, specifically: 
Outdoor, Terrestrial Uses 
“For terrestrial uses: Do not apply directly to water, or to areas where surface water is present or to intertidal 
areas below the mean high water mark. Do not contaminate water when disposing of equipment washwater 
or rinsate”. 
Outdoor, Residential Consumer Products 
For liquid concentrate formulations:  
“To protect the environment, do not allow pesticide to enter or run off into storm drains, drainage ditches, 
gutters or surface waters. Applying this product in calm weather when rain is not predicted for the next 48 
hours will help to ensure that wind or rain does not blow or wash pesticide off the treatment area. Rinsing 
application equipment over the treated area will help avoid run off to water bodies or drainage systems.” 
For broadcast granular formulations:  
“To protect the environment, do not allow pesticide to enter or run off into storm drains, drainage ditches, 
gutters or surface waters. Applying this product in calm weather when rain is not predicted for the next 48 
hours will help to ensure that wind or rain does not blow or wash pesticide off the treatment area. Sweeping 
any product that lands on a driveway, sidewalk, or street, back onto the treated area of the lawn or garden 
will help to prevent run off to water bodies or drainage systems.” 
For liquid ready-to-use formulations:  
“To protect the environment, do not allow pesticide to enter or run off into storm drains, drainage ditches, 
gutters or surface waters. Applying this product in calm weather when rain is not predicted for the next 48 
hours will help ensure that wind or rain does not blow or wash pesticide off the treatment area.” For products

with outdoor, terrestrial uses that require fish or aquatic invertebrate statements include: “Drift and runoff 
may be hazardous to aquatic organisms in water adjacent to treated areas.” 
 
• 
CASQA Recommendation:  CASQA supports EPA’s proposed label language mitigations for carbaryl. 
 
 
COMMENT #2:  CASQA SUGGESTS LABEL MITIGATION MEASURES FOR CONSISTENCY  
 
• 
CASQA recommends a small edit to label language to add greater clarity.   
o General Outdoor Application Statements [PID p. 55, App. B p. 84]: 
2. Perimeter band treatments of 6 ft wide or less from the base of a man-made structure to 
pervious surfaces (e.g., soil, mulch, or lawn) 
o CASQA’s suggested language: Perimeter band treatments to pervious surfaces (e.g., soil, 
mulch, or lawn) of 6 ft wide or less, measured from the base of a man-made structure 
 
• 
CASQA recommends correcting application rates in the PID mitigations to be consistent with the mitigations 
stated in the November 2022 BE Memo.  
o The PID notes [p.41] that: "Reducing the maximum annual application rate for turf to 16 lbs ai / 
acre (currently labeled maximum annual application rate for residential turf and golf courses is 36 
lbs ai / acre and 32 lbs ai / acre for sod)"  
o However, the BE Memo documents the pesticide registrants’ recommendations [Appendix C. 
Summary of Mitigations from Carbaryl Registrants for Listed Species, p. 85]:  
i. Ornamental Trees and Plants 
1. Maximum Annual Amount: 4 lbs. ai / acre (currently 6 lbs. ai / acre) 
2. Maximum Annual Number of Applications: 4 (currently 6 lbs. ai / acre) 
ii. Turfgrass (Golf Turf, Sports Fields, Sod Farms, Domestic and Commercial Lawns, 
Cemeteries, Parks, Campsites, Recreational Areas) 
1. Maximum Annual Amount: 10 lbs. ai / acre (currently 16 lbs. ai / acre) 
2. Maximum Application Rate: 5 lbs. ai / acre (currently 8 lbs. ai / acre) 
CASQA suggests correcting the maximum application rate values in the PID to match the values 
proposed in the BE Memo.  
 
• 
CASQA Recommendation:  CASQA suggests modifying the above label mitigations as noted above. 
 
CONCLUSIONS 
In summary, as documented in EPA’s risk assessments and PID, outdoor, non-agricultural uses of carbaryl may 
result in toxic concentrations of carbaryl in urban surface waters. Pesticide pollution of urban surface waters – 
causing toxicity to freshwater life – creates a multi-million-dollar regulatory burden for our municipal agency 
members. CASQA supports the inclusion of the proposed mitigation measures as enumerated in the PID. 
Thank you for your consideration of our comments. If you have any questions, please contact Victoria Kalkirtz, 
CASQA’s pesticides project lead, at (858) 541-4326 or vkalkirtz@sandiego.gov; or contact me at (424) 241-2249 or 
karen.cowan@casqa.org.

Carbaryl: Use and Benefits in the Desert Southwest  
and Response to EPA’s Proposed Interim Decision 
Prepared by Alfred J. Fournier, John Palumbo, Kai Umeda & Wayne Dixon  
Comments submitted by the Arizona Pest Management Center, 
University of Arizona 
 
Date: February 14, 2023 
Docket ID: EPA-HQ-OPP-2010-0230 
Re: EPA’s Proposed Interim Decision for Carbaryl  
 
To Whom it may concern: 
 
The EPA is seeking public comments in response its Proposed Interim Decision for the 
insecticide carbaryl. Carbaryl is registered for use on a wide variety of specialty crops, for use in 
outdoor residential pest control, ornamental plants, lawns and turf, rights of way, etc. Our goal at 
this time is to inform the EPA about a few remaining critical use patterns for carbaryl in Arizona 
and the Desert Southwest, and to respond to selected elements of the Proposed Interim Decision. 
 
At an earlier stage of registration review, we contributed detailed comments on the uses and 
benefits of carbaryl to the USDA Office of Pest Management Policy (Fournier et al. 2016). Some 
of our input was included in the benefits analyses for carbaryl. We have included key points 
from these prior comments in this response to EPA. In developing the current comments, we 
have examined updated use data and solicited information from stakeholders to verify ongoing 
use patterns. 
 
Summary 
• The use of carbaryl has diminished greatly in recent years across a wide variety of crops 
in Arizona and other parts of the Southwest. There are still selected uses for which 
carbaryl is deemed important and for which few or no viable alternatives exist.  
• Carbaryl is used, in rotation with pyrethroids, in the eradication program for the pecan 
weevil, an important invasive pest of pecans that has made recent incursions from West 
Texas into Eastern New Mexico. Loss of carbaryl would significantly impact the New 
Mexico Department of Agriculture’s ability to prevent or slow the spread of pecan weevil 
throughout New Mexico, and incursion into Arizona, California, and northern Mexico. 
We are grateful that EPA’s Proposed Interim Decision places no constraints on this use 
pattern. 
• Carbaryl bait formulations are used in Arizona in the management of darkling beetles, 
crickets, grasshoppers, and various soil insects on desert melons. Darkling beetles in

particular can devastate a stand of watermelon transplants, causing significant economic 
losses. This is not a frequent problem. We estimate that in Arizona fewer than 7% of

are available for control, particularly for darkling beetle.  
• Carbaryl is used in relatively rare situations to manage grasshoppers in turfgrass. Though 
not a frequent pest of desert turfgrass, grasshopper populations can migrate into 
residential turf from adjacent desert areas in large numbers, consuming seed from 
overseeding practices and damaging turf. Carbaryl bait is used as an effective means of 
control. If these baits are classified by EPA as granular pesticides, we recognize that EPA 
is proposing discontinuation of residential uses. We seek clarification on whether this 
mitigation would apply to Sevin 5 Bait applied by turf industry professionals working in 
residential settings. 
• Based on input from US Forest Service professionals, we agree with discontinuation of 
backpack sprays and with all additional proposed PPE requirements. While we recognize 
the need for EPA to limit the amount of solution handled for tree boring beetle treatment 
applications by US Forest Service to 250 gallons of solution per worker per day, the 
mitigation would in some case severely limit the timely treatment of tress, which could 
slow protection of forests from attack by tree boring beetles. In addition, we acknowledge 
that this mitigation will have economic consequences on beetle control practices by the 
US Forest Service. Carbaryl remains the most effective and longest lasting preventative 
treatment to protect Western forests from potentially devastating tree boring beetle 
infestations. 
 
 
Carbaryl Use on Arizona and New Mexico Crops & Turf 
The use of carbaryl has diminished greatly in recent years across a wide variety of crops in the 
Southwest. Based on information from the Arizona Pest Management Center (APMC) Pesticide 
Use Database (Fournier et al. 2017) from 2015 to 2021, only a small number of uses on limited 
acres have been reported. Uses include cantaloupes and other melons, fallow land, and very 
limited reported use on citrus and in turfgrass. Based on comments the Arizona Pest 
Management Center previously submitted to USDA Office of Pest Management Policy on 
carbaryl (Fournier et al. 2016), the most significant use in 2016 was as part of the eradication 
program for the pecan weevil in New Mexico. Carbaryl bait formulations are also used 
occasionally in Arizona in the management of darkling beetles and other insects in both 
transplanted and seeded melons. 
 
 
Carbaryl Use in Desert Melons 
In 2021, Arizona growers harvested 9,300 acres of cantaloupe and 4,900 acres of watermelon for 
the fresh market valued at over $124 million. (USDA 2022). In 2021, uses of carbaryl bait were 
reported on only 907 acres, about 6.4% of acres. Carbaryl is the Arizona Department of 
Environmental Management’s Groundwater Protection List, and all agricultural uses require 
reporting to the state. 
 
According to Dr. John Palumbo, Professor, Extension IPM Specialist, and Endowed Chair in 
Integrated Pest Management at University of Arizona, the main (occasional) use of carbaryl on 

 
3 
desert melons is the use of carbaryl bait targeting darkling beetles and other soil insects. Carbaryl 
bait is also sometimes used to control crickets and grasshoppers.  
 
Experience has shown that foliar sprays are ineffective for preventing darkling beetles from 
feeding on netted melons. Sprays cannot penetrate the foliage to get to the ground or undersides 
of melons where the beetles are active. The best chance of control is with the use of Sevin bait. 
There are no effective alternatives to carbaryl bait for this use. Gowan previously formulated a 
pyrethroid bait that was very effective, but it is no longer available on the market.  
 
Most applications of bait in the desert for darkling beetle control are applied pre-harvest. There 
are blooms in the field, but commercial pollinators have been removed by the time of 
application. The baits are spread on top of beds and must remain dry to be attractive to beetles. In 
the event that the bait got wet (e.g., rainfall), it is highly unlikely that the a.i. would move deep 
enough for soil uptake by the plant. Melon roots are deep in the soil profile by the time carbaryl 
would be applied. According to Dr. Palumbo, potential foliar alternatives for control of the 
darkling beetles prior to bloom include pyrethroids, neonicotinoids and methomyl. 
 
Some bait usage may occur pre-bloom, during stand establishment, to control soil insects. The 
use of sprinkler irrigation during stand establishment often precludes bait usage at this stage, but 
this practice can work well for drip-irrigated melons. In these cases, carbaryl is generally applied 
prior to transplanting, or at emergence for direct seeded melons. The most common alternative to 
carbaryl for this use is multiple applications of pyrethroids, whereas a single application of 
carbaryl bait provides effective control and lasts until the bait gets wet. 
 
One central Arizona grower I spoke with confirmed the importance of Sevin bait for control of 
darkling beetles in watermelon transplants. “Darkling beetles can and will devastate an 
expensive stand of watermelon transplants. It is not widely used, but for this pest, it is important. 
We do not use much active ingredient, but when we do it is vital!” (Fournier 2016). 
 
 
Carbaryl is Critical for Control of Invasive Pecan Weevil  
In 2021, pecans were the highest grossing crop in New Mexico, with 46,000 harvested acres 
valued at nearly $189 million (USDA 2021b). In 2015, over 2,000 New Mexico farms were 
involved in commercial pecan production, accounting for almost one third of pecans produced in 
the U.S. (Sutherland et al. 2017) In Arizona, 22,000 acres of pecans harvested in 2021 were 
valued at over $93 million (USDA 2021). 
 
As documented in detail in our 2016 comments to USDA Office of Pest Management Policy, 
carbaryl is critical to the eradication program for the pecan weevil, a destructive invasive pest.  
According to Sutherland et al., 2017: “Pecan weevil infestations can reduce nut yields 
significantly at two points in each growing season. In summer, adult weevils puncture and feed 
on immature nuts, causing these nuts to fall. Later in the growing season, females lay their eggs 
(up to six per nut) into larger, more mature nuts. Infested nuts cannot be salvaged. The adult 
stage is the only stage that is susceptible to insecticides. Eggs and larvae develop inside the 
maturing nuts where insecticides are not effective. Mature larvae emerge from nuts and burrow 
into the soil, as deep as 2–3 feet. No soil treatments are currently labeled for pecan weevil 

 
4 
larvae.” Due to the prolonged emergence period, multiple insecticide applications are required to 
control adult weevils.  
 
The pecan weevil is still intensively managed and is under quarantine in New Mexico (Garcia 
2023). According to Brad Lewis, Agricultural and Environmental Services Director at the New 
Mexico Department of Agriculture, New Mexico is considered the front-line battleground 
against this invasive pest. The department has successfully contained the pest within certain 
areas of the state and helped to prevent its spread farther west. Loss of carbaryl would 
significantly impact the department’s ability to slow the spread of pecan weevil throughout New 
Mexico, Arizona, California, and northern Mexico. The eradication program targets both 
commercial growers and residential plantings of pecans in monitoring for and treating pecan 
weevil (Garcia 2023).  
 
The repeated applications required for eradication of pecan weevil necessitate a rotational 
program. Carbaryl is the department’s primary rotational product when paired with a pyrethroid. 
Liquid formulations of carbaryl (e.g., Sevin 4F) are used in rotation with pyrethroids to 
control adult weevils after emergence. Lewis reported that typically, two applications of 
carbaryl are used in rotation with three applications of pyrethroids. Sevin 4f use rates 
were reported at 3 to 4 quarts/acre (Fournier et al. 2016).   
 
 
Response to Selected Proposed Mitigations for Carbaryl 
 
Citrus 
There have been very few reported uses of carbaryl in lemons over the past ten years, reportedly 
to control red scale. However, several knowledgeable licensed Pest Control Advisors (PCAs) 
who work with Arizona citrus growers say they either have never used carbaryl or have not used 
it over a decade in citrus. We do not expect the proposed rate reduction or additional personal 
protective equipment to negatively impact growers in Arizona.  
 
Turf  
According to Kai Umeda, Area Extension Agent in Turfgrass Science for University of Arizona 
(recently retired), carbaryl is used in relatively rare situations to manage grasshoppers in 
turfgrass. Though not a frequent pest of desert turfgrass, grasshopper populations sometimes 
build up in the desert after summer rains. As desert vegetation dries up, they can move into turf 
in residential areas adjacent to the desert large numbers, where they consume turf seed (from 
overseeding activities) and otherwise may feed on turf. On such occasions, pest control 
professionals providing contracted services may apply carbaryl (e.g., Sevin 5 Bait). It is one of 
few registered products and provides highly effective control. One to two applications may be 
needed to control grasshoppers. Multiple applications of registered pyrethroids could provide an 
alternative means of control.  
 
With respect to EPA’s proposed mitigation, “prohibit use on residential turf of granular 
formulations,” it is unclear to us whether EPA considers Sevin 5 bait (and generics) to be 
granular formulations. Based on current pesticide label information obtained through agrian.com, 
the Sevin 5 Bait label refers to the formulation as “bait,” whereas on a generic product label for 

 
5 
Drexel Carbaryl 5% Bait, the formulation is listed as “granules.” We request that EPA clarify 
whether the prohibition of granular formulations to residential turf includes applications 
of bait made by licensed professionals.  
 
We agree with EPA’s proposed maximum annual application rate of 16 lbs ai/A on turf. This 
would not be problematic, as one or two applications are sufficient to manage grasshoppers.  
 
We agree with EPA’s proposed prohibition on residential dust formulations of carbaryl. 
 
Forest Service Uses 
“The US Forest Service (USFS) reported treating <1% (approximately 800 acres) of all USFS 
land in the US with carbaryl annually from 2014-2018, to control wood-boring bark beetles on 
high-value or very vulnerable trees in forest lands managed by the USFS. All USFS treatments 
occurred west of the Mississippi River, primarily in the intermountain West and west of the 
Rockies.” (Mallampalli et al. 2022). Carbaryl has been described as “one of the most effective 
and environmentally safe insecticides used to prevent bark beetle attacks” (Hasting et al. 2001).    
 
According to Chris Fettig, Research Entomologist with the US Forest Service, Pacific Southwest 
Research Station, carbaryl remains a critical tool for the management of various tree boring 
beetles in Western forests. Fettig is a leading researcher on wood-boring bark beetle control in 
forests and has authored or co-authored numerous papers on this topic. In addition, we reached 
out contacts specifically familiar with current practices in Arizona forestry, including Alyssa 
McAlexander, Forest Health Specialist with the Arizona Department of Forestry and Fire 
Management and Joel McMillan with the USDA Forest Service Forest Health Protection 
Team based in Flagstaff, Arizona.  
 
In reviewing the EPA’s proposed mitigations on the use of carbaryl by USFS employees, these 
expert contacts offered the following insights.  
 
1. Prohibit backpack applications for tree boring beetle treatment applications by  
U.S. Forest Service (USFS).  
Experts we spoke with agreed with EPA’s proposed mitigation to discontinue use of 
backpack applications for tree boring beetle treatment by the U.S. Forest Service. 
Backpack applications are no longer typically used by the US Forest Service for 
treatment of tree boring beetles. The current emphasis is on preventative applications 
used in advance of beetle infestations to protect the trees. In such cases, larger equipment 
is used (Fettig et al. 2013). A common method of protecting trees from bark beetle attack 
is to saturate the tree bole with carbaryl using a hydraulic sprayer (Fettig et al. 2008). 
McMillan confirmed that loss of access to backpack sprays of carbaryl would not be 
problematic in Arizona for the same reason.  
 
In addition, both McMillan and McAlexander acknowledge that carbaryl use in Arizona 
is minimal compared to other Western states. Carbaryl has not been used to a large extent 
for wood boring beetle control in Arizona since the last severe infestation occurred 
around 2005. Beetle attacks are tied to severe drought events or other disturbances cause 
by weather conditions that can lead to large-scale tree loss if beetles are not properly 

 
6 
managed. While some level of drought has certainly persisted, we have not seen the 
large-scale and concerning level of damage and tree loss that drove the last wave of 
carbaryl applications. Currently, tree removal and other management techniques prevail 
to limit the spread of infestations. In addition, shortages of staff for large scale control 
efforts and the availability of alternative insecticides for management of tree boring 
beetles on a smaller scale were cited as other reasons why carbaryl use had declined. 
Permethrin or emamectin benzoate are the main insecticides used by homeowners or 
contractors in forested regions. Injections are preferred to spraying because effectiveness 
of injection is dependent on water flow, which can be controlled through irrigation. 
While research shows that carbaryl is more efficacious and lasts longer than alternatives, 
its use here has continued to decline for these reasons. 
 
2. Reduce amount of solution handled per worker per day for tree boring beetle 
treatment applications by USFS to 250 gallons of solution per worker per day.  
Fettig conveyed that the amount of carbaryl solution applied to a tree can vary a great 
deal, depending on a number of factors. “The amount of material (product + water) 
applied varies with bark and tree architecture, tree size, equipment and applicator, among 
other factors, but ranges from ~15 to 30 L per tree (roughly 4 to 8 gal.) under most 
circumstances. Application efficiency, the percentage of material applied that is retained 
on trees, ranges from ~80 to 90%.” (Fettig et al. 2013). Fettig expressed concerns that at 
the higher end of what may be needed for effective management, EPA’s proposed 
mitigation would severely limit the number of trees that could be treated per worker per 
day, which could slow protection of forests from attack by tree boring beetles.  
 
Joel McMillan was a participant in conversations with Cameron Douglass and others 
from USDA Office of Pest Management Policy in 2021 ahead of EPA finalizing this 
Proposed Interim Decision. He recalls that the 250 gallons of solution per worker per day 
was the consensus compromise among participants in those discussions. It was noted that 
this limitation would likely increase control costs, particularly for applications that are 
contracted out, since carbaryl sprays in some cases would have to be extended over 
multiple days to keep workers under the daily exposure limit. However, everyone 
acknowledges the importance of minimizing worker risk.  
 
3. Require double layer, gloves, PF10 respirator, chemical-resistant hat, and chemical-
resistant apron for beetle treatment applications.  
McMillan commented that it is likely in Arizona that USDA would contract out any 
future carbaryl applications and would develop contract specifications to ensure use of all 
required PPE by contractors.

Introduction 
On December 1, 2022, the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA or Agency) released its Carbaryl 
Proposed Interim Registration Review Decision1 (PID).  In addition to the standard FIFRA PID content, the 
proposed revisions document states: 
“Using its authorities under FIFRA, and in advance of completion of consultation with the 
Services, EPA is proposing mitigation for two pilot listed species for which the Agency 
predicts that there is a likelihood of Jeopardy (J) to these species or Adverse Modification 
(AM) to their designated critical habitats from the use of carbaryl.  2 
EPA also indicates that it is proposing certain alternative Reasonable and Prudent Measures (RPAs) for 
carbaryl to those described in the 2009 National Marine Fisheries Service (“NMFS”) Biological Opinion 
(“BiOp”).  EPA proposed to implement certain mitigations (e.g., wind directional buffers near Wireweed 
species range) and the alternative RPAs via its Endangered Species Protection Bulletins using EPA’s 
Bulletins Live! Two (BLT) system. 
TKI’s comments herein regarding the PID revisions and the proposed mitigations are intended to support 
development of a robust and defensible analysis of the unique potential risk of a pesticide, and to support 
integration of that analysis into localized mitigations that are spatially explicit, species-specific, and 
implementable by the user community.  TKI appreciates the opportunity to comment and provide 
additional information as the assessment of Jeopardy / Adverse Modification (J/AM) continues between 
the EPA and the Services and believes the registrant’s role in this process is instrumental in developing 
pragmatic and protective mitigations. 
The Role of Proactive Mitigations 
TKI agrees there are cases where mitigations such as those proposed in the revised PID may further the 
statutory objectives of both FIFRA and the ESA.  It is important, however, that any such proposed 
mitigations are based on the best available science and are feasible for end users to implement.  
Moreover, any such proposed mitigations would, in fact, supplement existing mitigations that currently 
support reduced exposure potential and which are implemented through mandatory label requirements. 
TKI is prepared to support proactive mitigations that are based on ecological risk assessments of sufficient 
detail to establish the need for, and positive impact of, such mitigations.  A J/AM assessment that indicates 
that some level of co-occurrence between an agricultural use site and species range or critical habitat 
might occur may not be sufficient to establish that mitigations prior to completion of a Biological Opinion 
are needed – even if the co-occurrence analysis is supplemented by a limited analysis of other risk factors, 
as described in the PID.  In the PID, predicted J/AM determinations are presented without any detailed 
assessment of estimated population-level effects.  Development of multiple lines of evidence relevant to 
the species being assessed, coupled with a population-level analysis that is then integrated into a weight 
of evidence framework is necessary when proactive mitigations are proposed.   
Proactive mitigations associated with regulatory actions may provide a rapid method of attempting to 
resolve ESA concerns in the PID.  However, there remains a clear need to direct resources into assessments 
that are well supported, reduce uncertainty, and that link the outcome of an assessment to specific 
mitigations.  The value and effect of proactive mitigations should also be clearly trackable and predictable 
in EPA decisions so that registrants can evaluate the merits of proactively developing mitigations in the 
future.

Addition of Bulletins Live! Two Language to Label 
Consistent with the Agency’s statement in the ESA Workplan3 that “when EPA expects that a pesticide in 
registration review may require mitigation implemented through Bulletins, the Agency will seek Bulletins 
language as part of the label it approves through an Interim Decision,” EPA indicates on p. 60 of the PID 
that it will require carbaryl labels to be updated to contain a standardized reference directing users to 
Bulletins Live! Two (BLT).  The statement indicates that the user must “obtain a Bulletin at any time within 
six months of the day of application” of the product and must comply with any required measures in such 
bulletin.  We refer to this language herein as the “BLT Reference.” 
TKI does not object to the use of Bulletins made available through BLT as a means of providing information 
regarding required mitigation measures.  In addition, TKI agrees with the concept of amending relevant 
pesticide labels to include the BLT Reference prior to finalization and publication of Bulletins on BLT.  
However, TKI has concerns with, and asks that EPA make clear that it is not proposing, a process whereby 
EPA can in the future make unilateral changes to Bulletins without consulting with, and obtaining approval 
from, registrants whose products will be impacted by such changes.  Such a procedure would be contrary 
to the structure and intent of FIFRA, and EPA’s longstanding practice and procedure regarding 
amendments to registered pesticides labels.  Changes to a Bulletin (or addition of a Bulletin) that would 
change the scope of a registration can only be accomplished with notice to, and approval from, the 
registrant.  EPA is now taking comments from TKI and others on the revised PID which may lead to 
alterations to relevant Bulletins that are completed as part of this registration review process.  The actual 
terms and requirements that are included in any such final Bulletin would be expected to reflect or at 
least be influenced by such comments.  This is the process (including final sign off by the registrant) that 
should be followed in the future should it be deemed appropriate to consider making changes to Bulletins 
that appear on BLT. 
TKI’s position is based on the fact that, once granted, a pesticide registration is a property right belonging 
to the registrant.  See e.g., Reckitt Benckiser, Inc. v. Jackson, 762 F. Supp. 2d 34, 45 (D.D.C. 2011) (“A FIFRA 
registration is essentially a license to sell and distribute pesticide products in accordance with the terms 
of the registration and the statute”).  Neither FIFRA nor the ESA grants EPA the right to unilaterally alter 
the scope of a FIFRA registration, once granted.  If EPA were to modify BLT without a registrant’s consent 
(even if the BLT Reference already appeared on the relevant label) it would be ultra vires and would 
contravene the structure of FIFRA.  Any modification to enforceable requirements for a pesticide’s use 
modifies the scope of that property right and hence the scope of the registration under FIFRA.  Moreover, 
such an action is expressly outside the scope of EPA’s authority under FIFRA, and Reckitt is instructive on 
this point.  Following an extensive review of the structure of FIFRA, as informed by the legislative history 
of numerous amendments of the statute in and after 1972, the Court in Reckitt concluded that EPA lacked 
authority to bring a misbranding action against a registrant, if the registrant refused to modify the 
registration of its product following an EPA conclusion that the existing registration no longer met the 
FIFRA standard for registration.  A cancellation proceeding under FIFRA 6(d) was the only proper recourse 
for EPA to follow if it chose to attempt to force the change.  As the Court stated, FIFRA “establishes a 
detailed, multi-step process that EPA must follow when it wants to cancel or suspend a registration.” 
Reckitt, 762 F. Supp 2d at 42.  This principle would apply also to a decision to unilaterally alter a substantive 
term or restriction in a Bulletin on BLT, if such Bulletin were considered by EPA to be an enforceable 
direction for use of the registered product. 
Therefore, the considerations in connection with an attempted unilateral change to a Bulletin on BLT by 
the Agency are the same – the Agency may not modify the scope of the registration without the 
registrant’s consent without utilizing the prescribed cancellation procedures in FIFRA.  Procedures for

In order to generate a relevant, predictable, and reliable representation of risk that justifies early 
mitigation, and that also indicates what, if any, mitigation measures might be appropriate, EPA must 
understand and apply information regarding regional and landscape-relevant product use, species natural 
history, and spatial relationships between likely habitat areas and potential product use sites.  In 
particular, the use of potentially suitable habitat to refine species ranges (based on spatially informed 
habitat characteristics) can greatly inform the likelihood of potential species locations and their 
vulnerability relevant to use sites.  This refinement offers a significant opportunity for targeted mitigations 
to be developed.  Without such refinement it will not be possible to identify specific locations that require 
protection and to develop justifiable, practical, and implementable mitigations that can be represented 
in Bulletins Live! Two. 
It is generally accepted that large portions of many defined ranges include areas within which species are 
unlikely to occur (e.g., waterbodies for land-dwelling species, urbanized areas for many species, 
elevation/climate restrictions, etc.) and because of this, further refinement to specific areas requiring 
protection within ranges is necessary.  As previously stated, TKI supports the use of information about 
potentially suitable habitat in addition to local information on species distribution to determine where 
listed species are most likely to occur and to inform specific mitigations in those areas.  A detailed analysis 
for suitable habitat within both range and critical habitat is often necessary for species, dependent on the 
reliability and relevance of areas defined as range or critical habitat. 
Carbaryl Historical Record Supports the Effectiveness of Existing Label Mitigations 
As expected for insecticides, carbaryl shows activity towards invertebrates.  However, there is a range of 
efficacy, and thus sensitivities, across invertebrate species.  As such, the consideration for “indirect 
effects” to listed species supporting constituents (e.g., prey, pollination, habitat, and dispersal functions) 
requires consideration for how this spectrum of efficacy might relate to invertebrate community-level 
effects at the magnitude that may result in listed species population level impacts or measurable impacts 
to a species critical habitat.  Carbaryl has a long history of safe use and the labels include numerous 
mitigations to reduce offsite transport and exposure to non-target species.  These mitigations support the 
safe use of carbaryl products to all non-target species, including listed species.

where EPA states that “[t]hese species-specific, geographically limited mitigations are expected to be

“To the extent that EPA conducts analysis to predict the likelihood of J/AM for all LAA

Comments on the Proposed Mitigations for the Wireweed 
For wireweed, EPA is proposing additional species-specific mitigations beyond the “baseline” EPA 
proposed label changes and voluntary mitigations proposed by the ag-use registrants.   
• 
No-spray buffers for applications of up to 200 feet between citrus orchards and the scrub habitat 
where the species is likely to be found.  This is based on overlap (39-44%) between citrus use sites 
and biologically relevant (based on lowest terrestrial invertebrate effects endpoints) deposition 
distances. 
• 
Limiting applications when bees are actively foraging and when crops or weeds within application 
sites are in bloom, intended to reduce exposure to wireweed pollinators on-field.   
Even with this proposed mitigation, EPA states that it would still conclude Jeopardy for the species.  
Therefore, an additional mitigation on citrus is proposed to avoid Jeopardy to wireweed as follows: 
In Polk county and Highland county, Florida, no-spray buffers are required between scrub 
habitat and citrus orchards if wind is blowing toward scrub habitat when applying 
carbaryl. The size of the wind-directional no-spray buffer is based on application rate as 
follows: 
1)  <1.0 lbs ai/A – do not apply within 50 feet of scrub habitat; 
2)  1.0-2.0 lbs ai/A – do not apply within 100 feet of scrub habitat; or, 
3)  >2.0 lbs ai/A – do not apply within 200 feet of scrub habitat. 
Wind directional buffers can be maintained at half the distance required above when windbreaks 
(e.g., trees or riparian hedgerows) between the application site and scrub habitat are present.  The 
windbreak would need to have a row of broad-leaved trees the full length of the treated crop with 
leaves visible over the entire length, with no significant gaps.  The height of the trees or windbreak 
would need to be at a height greater than the crop to be sprayed. 
TKI does not believe that a likelihood of Jeopardy to the wireweed is clearly established after the 
application of EPA-proposed label changes and the label changes voluntarily proposed by the ag-use 
registrants.  As such, TKI believes that the proposed EPA and registrant label changes are adequate 
without additional species-specific mitigations.  Additionally, as this pilot species and the species-specific 
mitigations focus on lines of evidence related to the wireweed, TKI does not believe that mitigations 
should be expanded to other species without a detailed endangered species assessment.   
EPA states that mitigations specific to the timing of wireweed bloom and reported elevation restrictions 
were considered in this pilot and that EPA opted for broader mitigations that would confer protections to 
other listed plant species with similar reliance on insect pollinators that co-occur in scrub habitat on the 
Lake Wales, Bombing Range, and Winter Haven ridges.  TKI provided EPA with a detailed analysis of 
potentially suitable habitat, as well as an analysis examining proximity between these areas and citrus

TKI supports species-specific localized mitigations when the likelihood of risk to populations from 
registered uses has been established.  As EPA states in the PID, the wireweed is a dicot plant and TKI

effects to wireweed are not anticipated for any of the currently registered uses of carbaryl.  Because dicot 
plants have been shown to be insensitive to carbaryl at and above labeled rates, the evaluation then 
focuses on the likelihood of community impacts to pollinators. 
TKI agrees that wireweed’s reproductive strategy is not entirely reliant on insect pollinators and the

It is not clear to TKI that a likelihood of Jeopardy due to impacts to pollinators has been established.  TKI 
does not agree with EPA’s assumption that 100% mortality of exposed terrestrial invertebrate individuals 
would result from application of carbaryl.  Terrestrial invertebrate sensitivity to carbaryl is wide ranging 
as indicated in the EPA’s Biological Evaluation of carbaryl.  Mortality data, based on endpoints expressed 
as mg/kg-bw, are available for 9 orders (i.e., Coleoptera, Dictyoptera, Diptera, Hemiptera, Heteroptera, 
Hymenoptera, Lepidoptera, Neuroptera, and Orthoptera), represented by 45 families, 68 genera, and 71 
species.  Based on this large volume of available data, carbaryl is associated with mortality of terrestrial 
invertebrates at concentrations ranging from 0.11 to >10,000 mg/kg-bw.  Terrestrial invertebrate 
mortality ranges from 0.0045 to ~18 lb/acre for studies conducted using lb/acre exposure units.  The data 
also demonstrate a range of sublethal impacts that may be associated with mortality from 0.0045 to >200 
lb/acre.  This indicates that there is a broad range of sensitivity to carbaryl and pollinators will likely appear 
across this range.  The PID assessment for wireweed focuses on the most sensitive terrestrial invertebrate 
endpoints; however, the entire range of sensitivities should be considered to evaluate possible pollinator 
community impacts that may translate to impacts to wireweed populations.  In addition, offsite transport 
effective distances are based on the most sensitive species, not the range of species, thus also 
overestimating effects potential.  This should be revised to consider the range of sensitivities. 
EPA also indicates that the wireweed is not expected to occur on agricultural use sites; however, the 
pollinator exposure analysis assumed wireweed pollinators will occur on agricultural use sites.  Due to 
standard agronomic practices, it is less likely that use sites would be attractive to pollinators when 
compared to many natural locations, and it is also unlikely that the majority of wireweed supporting 
pollinators would occur in these agricultural use areas.   
TKI supports EPA’s approach of emphasizing areas within the species range in which habitat or known 
populations of wireweed are more likely to occur.  TKI agrees that the wireweed distribution is restricted 
to a much smaller area within its delineated range and that evaluation of potential spatial overlap with 
known species locations is appropriate.  As stated in the pilot, the species is known to be endemic to Lake 
Wales, Winter Haven, and Bombing Range ridges in Polk and Highland counties with the majority (84%) 
of populations on the Lake Wales Ridge.  As indicated by EPA, most of these occurrences are within 
protected areas.   This is a significant line of evidence indicating unlikely exposure and risk potential to the 
species and pollinators in the vicinity of wireweed populations.   
TKI also supports EPA’s use of Percent Crop Treated (PCT) as a significant line of evidence in the 
assessment of potential exposure to listed species with its consideration of maximum PCT (i.e., that 
carbaryl is applied to all use sites) and average PCT (i.e., that carbaryl is applied on use sites consistent 
with state-level usage data) estimates.  TKI also agrees with EPA’s approach to evaluate each use site (i.e., 
UDL) in a manner that allows overlap and potential exposure between each of these areas to be evaluated.

Monitoring Conclusions Inconsistent with Monitoring Data 
In the pilot for the Upper Columbia River Steelhead Trout (UCRST), EPA stated that “The NMFS has 
identified pesticides are a potential concern for the UCRST and carbaryl is frequently detected in water 
monitoring samples and associated with one known fish kill incident in New Jersey.”  TKI examined national 
monitoring data from 2007 to 2021 available from EPA’s Water Quality Portal related to carbaryl 
concentrations in surface-water samples (Table 5).  The query included all sample fractions (dissolved, 
recoverable, extractable, and total), all results (accepted, preliminary, final, and historical), and actual and 
estimated values for carbaryl.  Over the 14 years examined, over 46,000 samples were recorded in the 
database. 
The overall non-detection rate for carbaryl was 90%, which does not support the NMFS assertion that 
“…carbaryl is frequently detected in water monitoring samples”.  Additionally, of the 10% of samples 
where carbaryl was detected, a maximum value of 14.1 µg/L (which was for extractable, not dissolved, 
carbaryl) was reported in 2016.  The next highest annual maximum values were 8.96 µg/L (2009), 6.69 
µg/L (2007), and 2.18 µg/L (2014).  Only seven of the 14 years examined had a maximum annual detection 
>1 µg/L, and only three years had a maximum annual detection >5 µg/L.  All detections over the 14 years 
were below relevant carbaryl effects thresholds for salmonids including the HC20 (17.1 µg/L) for aquatic 
invertebrates.  These results, based on over 46,000 samples tested for carbaryl, demonstrate that the 
likelihood of concentrations exceeding relevant effects thresholds are very limited.

Comments on the Proposed Mitigations to Implement NMFS 2009 Salmonid BiOp 
The PID states: 
“EPA concludes that the proposed FIFRA mitigation largely addresses the potential effects 
from the use of carbaryl to Pacific salmon and steelhead species. However, additional 
mitigation is needed for some application scenarios to implement NMFS BiOp.”26 
The NMFS 2009 Salmonid BiOp will be superseded by the upcoming BiOp scheduled to be released on 
June 30, 2023.  The mitigations proposed in the 2009 BiOp may not be consistent with what is proposed 
in the upcoming BiOp and implementing mitigations now based on the 2009 BiOp will likely lead to 
regulatory confusion.  TKI recommends that any mitigations ultimately proposed to implement the 
Salmonid BiOp be based on the upcoming 2023 BiOp, not the outdated 2009 BiOp. 
If, notwithstanding, the 2009 BiOp is implemented, the existing FIFRA mitigations combined with those 
listed in the PID proposed revision can provide appropriate protection of salmonid species / DPSs / ESUs, 
and no additional mitigations will be warranted.  However, if in the future additional mitigations such as 
restricted use buffers are considered necessary for carbaryl (or any other chemical), such mitigations 
should be based on a landscape-specific, spatio-temporal analyses suitable for refined exposure / effects 
characterization such as the work TKI submitted in support of the carbaryl salmonid pilot species.27,28 
Carbaryl PID Comments Conclusion 
TKI supports EPA’s efforts to appropriately and responsibly meet its obligations under both FIFRA and the 
ESA, and recognizes that in specific instances certain mitigations may be required to ensure that the 
statutory requirements of both FIFRA and the ESA are met.  However, TKI emphasizes that any mitigations 
that are proposed to be implemented must be based on the best available science and be spatially 
targeted to relevant areas.  Mitigations should also be practical, predictable and feasible for end users to 
implement.  In addition, any mitigations that are proposed to be implemented must have been developed 
taking into account existing mitigations that are already implemented through mandatory label 
requirements.  TKI looks forward to continuing to work with EPA and the Services to develop mitigation 
measures that are based on appropriate and adequate ecological risk assessments, and that reflect a 
weight of the evidence-based approach to species protection.

Thank you for the opportunity to comment on EPA’s proposed interim decision (PID) for

by Insecticide Resistance Action Committee (IRAC) as a Group 1A carbamate (IRAC, 2022). 
Carbaryl has wide usage and benefits in agriculture, particularly for use as a PGR on apples for

Rice—Proposed Use Prohibition 
 
While USDA generally agrees with EPA’s conclusion that carbaryl use on rice is of low average 
benefit nationally (USEPA, 2022a), we have concerns that EPA’s cancellation proposal will 
negatively impact growers in California that use carbaryl to control tadpole shrimp (UC-IPM, 
2015). For the remainder of rice uses in the mid-South, USDA received expert feedback that 
largely agreed with EPA’s characterization of low benefits for uses targeting rice stink bugs 
(Wilson, 2023; USEPA, 2022a). While pyrethroids are the primary tool for managing stink bugs, 
dinotefuran is a superior alternative option, with carbaryl reported to be not all that effective 
against stink bugs. While growers never like to lose tools for IPM, USDA generally has little 
concern about losing carbaryl for rice use outside of California. 
 
Tadpole shrimp management with carbaryl is a niche California need. While most California rice 
growers make primary use of pyrethroids (lambda-cyhalothrin and zeta-cypermethrin) (AMRD, 
2016-2020) to manage tadpole shrimp, carbaryl is an important alternative for management of 
pyrethroid resistance (Firoved, 2023). The use of copper sulfate is also reported in AMRD and 
recommended by extension experts alongside carbaryl, with chemical rotation emphasized as an 
important need (UC-IPM, 2015). Copper sulfate has some comparatively high and well-known 
risk concerns for aquatic taxa as well, though for organic rice producers, it may be the only tool 
for tadpole shrimp management. EPA’s ecological risk assessment for carbaryl modeled use on 
rice with two applications at the maximum label rate of 1.5 lb a.i./A with a 7 day retreatment 
interval and no holding time, based on reviews from data submitted for registration.  
 
Proposed Alternative Mitigation for Rice 
 
We wish to discuss the potential for a modified California-only use pattern for rice that would 
retain carbaryl for uses targeting tadpole shrimp, while still addressing many of EPA’s ecological 
exposure concerns on a national basis. Stakeholders have indicated to EPA that one early season 
application of carbaryl would be sufficient for their needs and that reasonable water holding 
times would be workable for growers, since the timing of this application would somewhat 
overlap with a number of herbicides that already require holding times (Firoved, 2023). 
Depending on a workable holding time restriction for carbaryl and how requirements intersect 
with herbicide needs, we believe this use of carbaryl could be adequately mitigated. Our 
preliminary estimates (for discussion with EPA) show these changes could reduce EECs by 
around 2.4-fold, for dissipation prior to release from the field. This is all before accounting for 
downstream dilution, which is not quantitatively incorporated into PFAM outputs. California 
stakeholders are willing to talk through some potential solutions with USDA and the Agency 
(Firoved, 2023) and we are happy to work through some possible options while still addressing 
any associated mitigation needs that arise for ESA consultation.  
 
Citrus—Proposed Application Rate Reductions, etc. 
 
USDA generally agrees with the Agency’s conclusions that on average, reducing the application 
rate of carbaryl for citrus will have limited impacts on growers, given low carbaryl usage 
(USEPA, 2022a). However, we note that low usage may not correlate with low benefits in this 
case, as the primary need for high rate carbaryl applications are for “rescue” treatments against

scale, particularly in instances where other control methods have failed (Cranney, 2023; Murden, 
2023). This benefit is also substantially increased since chlorpyrifos has been cancelled for all 
food uses, including citrus. Chlorpyrifos was a critical back-stop option for control of California 
Red Scale, and, in its absence, the alternative option of carbaryl for rescue treatments (UC-IPM, 
2022) has increased importance. When California Red Scale populations are high, many 
alternative insecticide options can fail, despite best efforts by growers, making carbaryl the last 
effective line of defense (Cranney, 2023).   
 
The use of carbaryl for scale species is mostly an issue in California and Texas, as carbaryl 
applications targeting scale are far less common in Florida. However, carbaryl has a different 
benefits profile for Florida growers, as it is used to target adult stages of Diaprepes root weevils 
(Diepenbrock, 2023). Weevil larvae feed in the soil and can girdle roots and/or vector fungal 
infections that can kill the host, including citrus trees (Weissling et al., 2019). While carbaryl is 
not applied to soil to target larvae, it is an effective tactic for controlling adults that live in the 
tree canopy, for reduction of weevil populations (Diepenbrock, 2023). AMRD indicate the 
average carbaryl application rate for weevil management on Florida citrus is approximately 3.2 
lbs AI/acre. However, based on a rate range analysis, USDA notes that approximately 15% of 
carbaryl applications to Florida oranges and grapefruit targeting root weevils are made at or 
above 6 lbs AI/acre (AMRD, 2016-2020). While research is ongoing to find effective alternative 
control methods for weevils, retention of carbaryl flexibility remains important for this pest. 
 
Proposed Alternative Mitigation for Citrus 
 
USDA understands that while the proposed application rate reduction for citrus (to 5 lbs AI/acre) 
is driven by occupational risk concerns (since bystander drift could be addressed with a small 
off-field drift buffer, even at 12 lbs AI/acre), restoring higher application rates for citrus may 
complicate ongoing consultation discussions with USFWS and NMFS. We therefore propose 
that for areas within 300m of NMFS species habitat, keeping the rate reduction to 5 lbs AI/acre 
would be workable and would not fundamentally change the ‘action’ under consideration. This 
would then allow for focus on occupational mitigation options and potentially allow the Agency 
to maintain rate flexibility for the remaining citrus acreage that is not near ESA habitat.  
 
For airblast applications to citrus, the exposure estimates and MOEs are driven by an assumption 
of treating 40 acres per day. The combined total MOE (driven by dermal exposure) for 
applicators using DL/G/CRH and a PF-10 respirator at a rate of 12 lb ai/A is 7.4 with a target 
MOE of 10 and increases to 70 and is not of concern when applicators use engineering controls 
(enclosed cabs). USDA notes that enclosed cabs are typically used for airblast applications in the 
citrus industry. Additionally, because citrus applications require very high water volumes per 
acre (often at or exceeding 500 gallons per acre), there is considerable daily downtime for 
airblast applicators due to the need to refill sprayer tanks more often. Therefore, USDA suggests 
that EPA consider requiring an enclosed cab for citrus airblast applications or setting a daily 
acreage application limit for applications higher than 8 lbs AI/acre if an enclosed cab is not used 
because it would address EPA’s occupational risk concerns while still allowing flexibility for 
growers occasionally needing to target scale in California (or possibly also weevils in Florida) 
with higher application rates. For example, USDA has estimated that combined airblast 
applicator MOEs would be 11 if applicators wore SL/G/CRH and a PF10 respirator and treated 
27 acres per day at an 8 lb ai/A rate or wore DL/G/CRH and a PF10 respirator and treated 27 
acres per day at a 12 lb ai/A rate. Lower daily acreage would not be needed for applicators using 
an enclosed cab. Application acreage restrictions have been successfully used for other recent

USDA is concerned about the impacts of EPA’s proposed 18-day REI for cut flowers grown

applications to flowers. While we agree with EPA’s statement that most cut flower production 
occurs indoors, USDA notes that small outdoor operations (including pick-your-own retail

Pollinator Protection 
 
USDA is concerned that EPA’s current proposal is overly restrictive for granular carbaryl bait 
products applied to the ground in plantings of tomatoes and melons, for control of ground 
beetles. This use was not explicitly discussed by EPA in terms of product type and formulation, 
though it was acknowledged as a pest management need (USEPA, 2022a). Indeed, carbaryl 
granular baits are a critical need for control of ground beetles and other soil surface pests in 
tomato (Bagely, 2023) and melon production (Fournier, 2023; Palumbo, 2023). Baits are spread 
on the soil surface and need to remain dry to be attractive to beetles. Dr. Palumbo emphasized 
the specific IPM need, reporting that no viable alternatives are available to replace the loss of 
carbaryl bait and that the beetles and other soil pests targeted by baits can directly damage 
melons. Various experimental pyrethroid products have been evaluated, but these products either 
never became commercially available or were removed from the market (Palumbo, 2023). 
Sprays are also inadequate to manage beetles because it’s too difficult to penetrate the foliage 
and get to the ground or undersides of fruit where beetles are most active (Palumbo, 2023). 
 
We believe a bloom restriction on granular bait products is unwarranted and contend that some 
usage and exposure characterization can address the low likelihood of pollinator risks for 
granular baits. For melons, while many bait applications are made pre-harvest, there can be 
instances of straggling, indeterminate bloom present in fields during this time, even if 
commercial bees have long since been removed from fields. Available usage data for cantaloupes 
and watermelons (AMRD, 2016-2020) also indicate that significant carbaryl bait usage occurs at 
planting or shortly after planting. While this can be prior to bloom, the definitions of these crop 
stages can vary and it would be impossible to preclude all bloom presence during important 
application windows. For tomatoes, experts indicated to USDA that much of the need for baits 
was at transplanting or shortly after planting (Bagely, 2023). However, available usage data also 
shows a significant amount of bait usage reported during periods that could coincide with bloom, 
since tomatoes also bloom indeterminately (AMRD, 2016-2020). In all cases, the predominant 
products used in-season on tomatoes and melons are granular baits, and foliar carbaryl sprays are 
not widely used.

USDA wholly supports a restriction on foliar carbaryl sprays for these crops during bloom, but

especially given the benefits of carbaryl for this important pest management need. 
 
USDA urges EPA risk managers to consider some additional weight of evidence for this scenario 
and exempt granular bait products from the proposed bloom restriction. We contend that if 
carbaryl had meaningful systemic activity as assumed, IPM researchers and chemical companies 
would have long ago pursued registration for use patterns taking advantage of such efficacy and 
would apply carbaryl to soil accordingly. Dr. Fournier notes he “wasn’t aware that carbaryl had 
soil systemic activity. Even if it did, the baits are spread on the bed top and need to remain dry to 
be attractive to beetles.  In the event that the bait got wet (e.g., rainfall) It is highly unlikely that 
the a.i. would move deep enough for soil uptake.” USDA further contends that any watering-in 
of carbaryl bait granules would actually undermine efficacy, so great care is taken to avoid this 
scenario. In fact, early season use of granules is precluded for some crops due to irrigation 
demands. In order for these baits to be effective, they must remain dry and on the soil surface, 
where ground beetles, earwigs, and other target pests can contact them directly. Because bees are 
flying insects attracted to blooms, we do not believe there is reason to suspect attraction to bait 
granules or any widespread, persistent exposure to carbaryl residues on the soil surface via 
ground foraging. 
 
We otherwise broadly support EPA’s proposed verbiage and bloom restriction approach for 
foliar carbaryl applications on other crops, given the acute toxicity risks posed for bees by 
carbaryl exposure. We especially appreciate EPA’s considerations and proposed verbiage

Mitigation Proposals Addressing Select Endangered Species 
 
Soil Saturation and Rainfall/Runoff Events 
 
Similar to comments submitted in response to EPA’s revised PID for methomyl (USDA, 2022) 
we have concerns around EPA’s proposed rain restrictions as written, mainly pertaining to clarity 
of the term “field capacity”. We support the intent and use of the proposed statement as a 
workable runoff mitigation strategy. We further appreciate EPA specifying that applications 
cannot be made to “saturated” soil vs. simply “wet” or “moist” soil, as we believe saturated soil 
poses the most reasonable scenario for runoff if additional precipitation were to immediately 
follow a pesticide application. However, experts in consultation with USDA have noted that 
“saturation” and “field capacity” have different meanings and that farmers will more clearly 
understand the former. 
 
“Saturation” is considered to be the soil water content when all pores are filled with water (UNL, 
2022). “Field capacity,” on the other hand, is technically the soil water content after the soil has 
been saturated and allowed to drain freely for 24-48 hours (in other words, the amount of water 
that remains in soil after draining all gravitational water) (Farsad, 2019; UNL, 2022; USDA, 
2008). In the strictest sense, these two terms have different meanings, and USDA would suggest 
that EPA simply use “saturated” as this term is thought to be more widely understood by growers 
(Meyers, 2022). USDA suggests the following alternative language: 
 
“Do not apply carbaryl products when soils are saturated.” 
 
Other stakeholders have voiced similar concerns to USDA regarding the clarity of the restriction 
around future storm events. There is broad consensus among both IPM experts and State Lead 
Agencies (SLAs), as expressed to USDA, that such a statement is confusing and difficult for 
growers to comply with as currently proposed. Much of this feedback has been previously shared 
with EPA for other registration review cases, most recently for atrazine. First, the word “likely” 
provides limited information to either growers or applicators who want to comply with pesticide 
labels, or to SLAs responsible for enforcing this mitigation. Secondly, a “runoff-producing 
storm” means something different depending on a wide variety of landscape, temporal, 
environmental, and soil factors, and weather forecasts will not provide growers a distillation of 
all of these factors in a useful manner. Lastly, stakeholders suggested that EPA needs to narrow 
the permissible sources of forecast information. USDA suggests that the National Oceanic and 
Atmospheric Administration’s (NOAA) National Weather Service (NWS) provides the highest- 
quality, most transparent, and reliable forecasts available for the US, therefore requests EPA to 
point growers solely towards NOAA/NWS forecasts available at weather.gov for information 
related to the chance of runoff-producing rainfall. 
 
USDA reached out to several climatologists located in the Midwest for their feedback on this 
proposed label language, and they concurred with the concerns expressed by weed scientists and 
extension specialists. The climatologists that USDA spoke with recommended that instead EPA 
would ideally move forward with more specific language that included the following elements: 
use of the term “rainfall” instead of “storm” or “storm event”; a probability (i.e., a percentage 
chance of a runoff-producing rainfall within 48 hours); and specifically citing the use of

Wind-Directional Dependent Drift Buffers 
 
In particular, we strongly support EPA’s proposal to make spray drift buffers conditional on the 
wind blowing toward habitat by using the following statement: “Do not apply . . . within ____ 
(distance) of habitat if the wind is blowing in the direction of the habitat” (emphasis added). 
While this qualifier may seem obvious to some parties, its inclusion provides growers with a 
valuable margin of flexibility to wait out weather conditions for more optimal application 
conditions. As such, USDA believes the clause actively incentivizes producers to choose 
application timings that minimize the potential for drift. In contrast, a full-time buffer imposed 
without regard to wind direction provides no such incentive because the restriction and entailing 
impacts exist regardless of local conditions. From a practical standpoint, the more flexible 
approach focuses the buffer requirement on situations where mitigation is needed to minimize 
off-field exposure (i.e., when the wind isn’t already doing that job by default). In the absence of 
this clause, growers would face more difficult choices about alternatives or taking significant 
areas out of production in order to comply with an immovable, always-present, one-size-fits-all 
buffer zone.  
 
Growers and their representatives have consistently responded to EPA (via public surveys as 
well as personal communications) that altering their spray timings to minimize drift is a common 
practice and among the most compatible options much of the time. While we understand that 
there will still be some negative impacts to some producers in areas near species habitat (for 
example, in areas where persistent winds are difficult to avoid), we think this impact is not likely 
to be widespread for most producers or for all crops.  
 
Specifically pertaining to spray buffers, we appreciate and support EPA’s proposed approach for 
mitigating wireweed exposure by using wind-directional, rate-dependent spray buffers for scrub 
habitats in Highland and Polk Counties. Available data (USDA, 2019) indicate that these 
counties combined accounted for approximately 25% of citrus acreage and 32% of citrus 
production in 2017. A leading expert from Florida opined that the proposed buffers should not
