Proposed Airblast Drift Buffer for Upper Columbia River Steelhead Trout Habitat 
 
USDA is concerned about EPA’s inconsistent (or perhaps inadvertent) proposal to have airblast 
drift buffers (40 feet) from aquatic habitat differ from other ground applications (25 feet) for the 
instances when wind is not blowing toward habitat. We appreciate EPA’s approach and fully 
support the design and intent (as described above) for wind directional buffers and also support 
having larger buffers apply when wind is blowing toward aquatic habitat. We have no concerns 
with the proposed 55-foot buffer when wind is blowing toward habitat. However, we are 
confused as to why a number higher than 25 feet would be required for the instances when wind 
is blowing away from habitat. None of the AgDrift parameters or chemical characteristics (i.e., 
inputs impacting the proportion of the drift fraction reaching water) would apply in instances 
where the wind is already preventing drift by default, by blowing away from habitat. 
 
We note the 40-foot proposal is a mismatch from the ESA mitigation applied for airblast 
applications of malathion and diazinon, both of which had a starting point of 25 feet as a baseline 
buffer (which USDA supports) for aquatic habitat, and then additional buffer distances applied 
when wind is blowing toward habitat. Selecting 40 feet is also inconsistent with the mitigation 
proposed in this same carbaryl PID for protection of wireweed/scrub habitat in Florida, where 
rate-dependent buffers also only applied to situations where the wind is blowing toward habitat. 
From a practical standpoint, we believe that consistency in this approach and adopting a baseline 
buffer of 25 feet from aquatic habitat for all ground uses, as proposed earlier for drift mitigation, 
is a workable, predictable, and effective approach. We don’t believe it detracts at all from actual 
real-world protection, since larger buffers can (and will) still apply for the instances where drift 
is actually being directed to the habitat of concern by winds. We request EPA revise the draft 
mitigation for airblast uses accordingly to “Do not apply within 25 feet of aquatic habitats….” 
and retain “If the wind is blowing toward aquatic habitat, do not apply within 55 feet of aquatic 
habitats….” We are happy to discuss further with EPA, NMFS, and FWS to arrive at workable 
statements that adequately protect all species while not imposing unnecessary burdens or 
uncertainty on producers. 
 
Species Range Maps 
 
USDA encourages EPA to use the most up-to-date species range maps in all of their analyses, 
and notes that EPA does not clearly reference the versions used in the carbaryl documents 
(USEPA, 2022a, 2022d). Use of the updated maps would also be consistent with the FWS 
approach to determining J/AM in the malathion BiOp. With approximately 1,000 range maps

that implications of any changes to the range are apparent.

USDA commends EPA on this proposal for ESA mitigation. We find it to be reasonable and 
compatible with growers’ existing practices, and something that confers tangible, durable, and 
enforceable protections against drift exposure to species habitat on pesticide labels. USDA

Dear Ms. Romanovsky: 
 
We are writing to you on behalf of the American Sugarbeet Growers Association (ASGA), the 
U.S. Beet Sugar Association (USBSA), and the Beet Sugar Development Foundation (BSDF) to 
provide comments on the U.S. EPA’s recently released Carbaryl Proposed Interim Registration 
Review Decision, Case Number 00800 (Carbaryl PID). We appreciate that EPA is seeking input 
on this document; however, in the future we would ask that EPA consider a longer public 
comment period so that we have sufficient time to engage all our growers who may use carbaryl.         
 
We represent the 10,000 family farmers in 11 states that raise sugarbeets on 1.0 million acres and 
cooperatively own all 21 factories in the U.S. that process sugar from sugarbeets. We also 
represent these cooperatives and the four sugarbeet seed-related companies in their active beet 
sugar research and education. Collectively, we produce over half of all domestically produced 
sugar. The U.S. beet sugar processing industry is 100 percent farmer-owned and cooperative in 
structure, and every factory operates with organized union workers. 
 
The U.S. beet sugar industry has become a global leader in environmental sustainability as we 
have invested in significant programs that preserve our natural resources, family farms, 
unionized workforces, and rural communities for future generations. As a result, our industry 
now produces 29 percent more sugar on eight percent less land than 20 years ago, and sugarbeets 
now require significantly less land, water, and fuel. Growers have optimized pesticide use so that 
it affects fewer off-target organisms. 
 
While carbaryl is not widely used by all our growers, for those that use it, it provides important 
protections. Below we provide comments on a few aspects of the proposed mitigations. 
 
Pollinator Mitigation Language 
 
While sugarbeets do not flower, we are concerned about the language EPA uses on page 53 of 
the Carbaryl PID which states, “Alternatively, when plants in adjacent areas are in bloom, the 

Agency is considering only allowing applications of carbaryl within two-hours of sunrise or two-
hours of sunset, limiting the application window to eight hours per day.” EPA should clarify 
whether “plants in adjacent areas” includes weeds or vegetative buffers. 
 
Similarly, in discussing bloom restriction, on page 85 EPA states, “Notifying beekeepers within 
1 mile of treatment area at least 48 hours before product is applied will allow them to take 
additional steps to protect their bees. Limiting applications to times when bees are least active, 
e.g., within 2 hours of sunrise or sunset, will minimize risk to bees.” This will be very difficult 
for our growers to achieve, and it is also impractical since weather patterns can change within 
hours making an application possible or impossible. 
 
Proposed Water Protection Statements and Proposed Rain-Related Statements 
 
Carbaryl has a chemigation label; therefore, parts of the proposed water protection and rain-
related protection statements might be hard to achieve, in particular, both “[d]o not apply or 
irrigate to the point of run-off” and “[d]o not apply carbaryl products when soils are saturated or 
above field capacity.” Both of these applications could happen after a longer irrigation set. EPA 
should clarify whether these mitigations apply to chemigation. 
 
Application Rate Units 
 
In Appendix D, application rates are in pounds. We use products that provide application rates 
using quarts of product per acre. We recommend that EPA allow both on the label.  
 
Proposed Bulletins Live! Two (BLT) Limitation Language 
 
It is important that EPA recognizes that our growers have never before had to use BLT. Thus, the 
use of this webpage and the understanding of how to navigate it and how to apply it is 
completely novel. If requirements for BLT were added to future pesticide labels, our growers 
would require new training and education to understand how to use BLT. If EPA intends to use 
BLT with every new label, we recommend that EPA starts planning training and outreach to 
growers to help ease the transition and facilitate an easier understanding. Our members would be 
willing to participate in a focus group setting to help EPA better understand how to communicate 
this tool to us and other growers. 
 
While we have not used the tool previously, we can unequivocally state that a six-month lead 
time is not sufficient to plan for planting and associated needs. Our growers make land deals, 
plan crop rotations, modify tillage practices, and buy pesticide products at least a year in 
advance. If EPA requires that BLT be reviewed within six months of pesticide application, these 
critical decisions would be made before any BLT review. It would be potentially very 
challenging and burdensome to implement BLT if it requires changes to crop placements and 
planned pesticide applications. We recommend that EPA allows at least one-year lead time for 
implementing BLT requirements. Additionally, our understanding is that BLT often depicts very 
large areas for use limitations. We recommend that EPA try to be as specific as possible when 
using BLT and require use limitations only when absolutely necessary. 
 

Salmonid Proposed Alternative Mitigations 
 
Regarding the runoff reduction options list A (page 64), we are concerned that a 65 foot buffer is 
far too much land to give up. This would have concerning economic impacts. We recommend 
that EPA should consider a 25-foot buffer or less. Additionally, we believe the spot application 
would likely only be rarely used. 
 
Other runoff options EPA may want to consider would include field borders, cover cropping, and 
no/reduced tillage. While not all our growers can use these practices, having additional options 
would be helpful to some of our growers.  
 
Conclusion 
 
We appreciate the opportunity to comment on the considered mitigations and would be pleased 
to provide EPA with any additional information that may be helpful. If you have additional 
questions, please contact Carrie Meadows at carrie.meadows@beetsugar.org, Zack Clark at 
zclark@americansugarbeet.org, or Anna Murphy anna@bsdf-assbt.org.

crop canopy, thereby not disrupting the crop and damaging it. The productivity, accuracy, speed, 
and lack of damage to the crop has been recognized in Europe as well2. Although the average

these small businesses treat nearly 127 million acres of U.S. cropland each season, which is

Wind-direction-based buffers zones will minimize impact to growers because these areas can 
still be treated by aerial applicators when the wind is blowing away from the endangered species 
and their critical habitat. The buffers will also fully protect sensitive areas from spray drift 
because they will be implemented when the wind direction is towards the sensitive site. They 
provide a win-win solution that balances the needs for optimum agricultural production and 
protection of listed species and sensitive habitats. Furthermore, allowing for the area near field 
borders to be treated once the wind shifts away from a sensitive area will enable greater crop 
yields resulting in less land needed for agricultural production and leaving more land available 
for endangered and threatened species habitat.   
 
Aerial applicators have the tools necessary to provide immediate and onsite wind direction 
measurement, so if wind direction does change during the application, they can respond 
immediately. Aerial applicators can monitor weather conditions in the cockpit and thus evaluate 
the need for a buffer zone in real time using a smoker or AIMMS. A smoker injects a small 
amount of vegetable oil into the aircraft exhaust system that creates smoke, allowing the pilot to 
determine, by observing smoke movement, the wind direction, and an estimate of wind speed. 
Inversions can also be detected by observing vertical smoke movement. The Aircraft Integrated

“Scientific name: Triops longicaudatus 
Common name: Tadpole Shrimp 
DESCRIPTION OF THE PESTS 
Although they are crustaceans, tadpole shrimp resemble tadpoles in size, shape, color, and 
mobility. Tadpole shrimp have about 35 body segments, and all but the last six or seven have 
pairs of leaflike, gill-bearing appendages. A thin, olive-brown shield covers the front section 
of the body, and two long tails extend from the last segment. Two long, jointed appendages 
resembling antennae extend from below the well-developed chewing mandibles. 
Adults deposit eggs singly on soil or on plants at the bottom of the field. They are highly 
resistant to drying and remain viable for several years in unflooded soil. Most of the eggs 
hatch 1 to 3 days after spring flooding of the rice fields, but hatching may continue for 1 to 2 
weeks. The young develop rapidly by a series of molts and resemble the adults in less than 
24 hours. They feed on a variety of small animals and plants commensurate with their size 
as they grow and molt. The somewhat transparent molt skins may be mistaken for dead 
shrimp. The first instar larva is about 0.2 inch (5 mm) long. Egg pouches are first noted 
when shrimp are about 0.63 inch (16 mm) long, and by 3 weeks old the shrimp may be 1 
inch (2.5 cm) long. At maturity, tadpole shrimp are about 1.5 inches long. Masses of red-
orange eggs occur in 7 to 10 days from hatching in two brood pouches on the appendages of 
the 11th segment at the lower margin of the shield. 
DAMAGE 
Tadpole shrimp cause losses in seedling rice stands in two ways. First, they may chew off the 
coleoptile, roots, and leaves of the seedling, and uproot seedlings with their digging and 
feeding activity, all of which may kill the plants. Second, their digging activities associated 
with egg laying muddy the water, reducing light penetration and thereby slow the growth of 
the submerged seedlings. Tadpole shrimp cause no injury to rice once leaves have reached 
the water surface and roots are well established in the soil.

MANAGEMENT 
Management of tadpole shrimp involves rapid seeding of the field after flooding and 
monitoring twice within the first 2 weeks following flooding to determine the need for 
chemical treatment. As an alternative, some population reduction can be obtained by 
flooding and draining the field before flooding for seeding. 
 
Cultural Control 
 
Most tadpole shrimp eggs hatch within 2 days after contact with water. The longer the time 
between hatching of the eggs and planting, the larger the size of the shrimp and the greater 
the potential for plant injury. Flood the field as fast as possible, and seed as soon as possible 
after flooding has been initiated. In very large fields that take more than a few days to flood, 
you may want to seed basins (checks) in sequence as they fill with water. Rice stands that 
have been reduced by shrimp feeding can be reseeded but generally a good stand of rice is 
difficult to establish in this manner. 
 
Flooding and draining the field before planting will kill hatched tadpole shrimp through 
desiccation and are alternatives to chemical control. Do not drain the field until 4 to 5 days 
after initial flood so the maximum egg hatch can occur. The draining time will vary based on 
soil type and weather but should continue for at least 24 hours after all standing water is 
gone. Shrimp will gather in standing water in low areas and will reinfest the field if the drain 
period is too short. Reflooding may result in some shrimp from previously unhatched eggs, 
but they would be in noneconomic numbers and less likely to damage the older, firmer 
rooted seedlings. Any soil cultivation following the drain period may bring viable, unhatched 
shrimp eggs to the soil surface for possible infestation upon reflooding, however. 
 
A decision to drain must take into account possible negative aspects such as fertilizer loss, 
encouragement of weeds, or interruption of weed control procedures, interruption of 
pesticide holding requirements, and the economics of irrigation. 
 
Organically Acceptable Methods 
 
Draining, as described under cultural controls, and applications of copper sulfate are 
organically acceptable methods. 
 
Monitoring 
 
Check all your fields during seedling development, but give special attention to those that 
had significant populations of tadpole shrimp last year. Even though infestations may have 
been localized in previous years, monitor all quadrants of the field because the shrimp can 
occur well beyond previously observed boundaries. Masses of wind-blown cut leaves and 
floating seedlings along the levees combined with muddy water are good evidence of

IV. Cultural Practices 
 
In the Central Valley north of Sacramento, the majority of rice is grown on clay soil primarily 
unsuitable for supporting other crops (CH2M Hill 1992.) Therefore, crop rotation is not 
common on rice ground. Approximately 98 to 99 percent of California rice is seeded in 
standing water at three to five inches deep. The field preparation and rice planting are 
weather dependent. Weather can delay the planting process, but there never is a time when 
the season starts early due to unusually dry conditions as the temperatures are too cool for 
germination, and the early planted rice becomes feed for late migrating waterfowl. 
 
 
 
A. Field preparation 
 
Water can be held on the harvested (non-crop period) rice fields over the winter months 
with draining starting at the end of February, first of March. The harvested fields usually fill 
from rainfall. These wet fields facilitate the decomposition of the stubble remaining after 
harvest. The winter flooded fields provide habitat for migration waterfowl along the Pacific 
Flyway.

Page 8 of 12 
 
Food to sustain the waterfowl comes from spent grain left from the harvester, and insects 
living in the mud. With the loss in wetlands for flood control, the rice fields provide 300,000 
acres of winter habitat. Considerable research in collaboration with the industry, the 
Universities, and several avian groups demonstrate the benefits rice fields provide to 
wildlife. Section V cites some of the decades of work and studies on impacts to waterfowl.  
 
After the field is drained, the soil is disked to open up the top layer allowing it to aerate. 
Additional equipment is used to break-up the disked soil into a finer, smoother texture. 
Preplant fertilizer is incorporated at this time. The fields are leveled to slopes of 0.05 to 0.1 
percent to allow for drainage. A grooved roller is pulled over the leveled field to create small 
rolls of ridges (UCCE/UCANR, Land Formation 2015).  
 
Water is then added to the field at a depth of three to five inches. The rice seed is soaked in 
water 24 to 48 hours before planting. Soaking the seed starts the germination process and 
adds weight. The soaked seed is flown onto the field dropping through the water and settling 
into a groove formed during field preparation.  
 
Seedlings will break through the water and remain vulnerable to insect infestation, or 
dislodging until the plant tillers and begins forming the canopy. Once the rice stand is 
established, the plant is naturally resistant to insect infestation under normal conditions 
(UCCE/UCANR 2015, Planting & Stand Establishment).

B. Rice seeding 
 
Approximately one to two percent of California rice is dry seeded. Dry seeding helps to 
break up the weed cycle due to the limited number of available herbicides with differing 
modes of action.

Water seeding became an industry wide practice around 1982 (Div. of Ag. Sci. 1982). The 
initial rational was to allow the pre-germinated seed an opportunity to break the water 
surface in advance of the weeds for non-chemical control. In addition to weed control, water 
seeding facilitates nitrogen nutrition and increases productivity. The rice seed is water 
soaked 24 to 48 hours in large bins that are drained before the seed is transferred to trucks 
and delivered to the fields. The seed is transferred from the truck to an airplane and flown 
onto the prepared, flooded field. 
 
The water is kept on the field throughout the season except for short-term drainage, 
permanently removing it only at the end of the growing season to prepare the crop for 
harvest. Water depth is maintained at three to five inches for three or more months 
depending on the pest pressure to the crop.  
 
As previously stated, California rice is most susceptible to damage during the first six weeks 
after seeding, the time it takes for the crop to set roots and break through the water. 
Growers refer to this critical time as stand establishment when the plants are most 
vulnerable to insect pressure (UCCE/UCANR 2015, Planting & Stand Establishment; 
UCCE/UCANR 2015, Water Management). 
 
Whether rice growers water or dry seed, the water is added and cultural practices are 
identical for the growing season. The flooding of rice fields during the production stage 
involves the same practices whether the crop was dry, or water seeded.  
 
The number of plants per square foot can vary from 12 to 46 (UCCE/UCANR 2015, Planting 
and Stand Establishment). Minimum seedling population for maximum yield is dependent 
on many factors including sowing method, water management, planting date, rice variety 
and soil type (UCCE/UCANR 2015, Planting & Stand Establishment).

CropLife America Comments on the Proposed Interim Registration Review Decision for Carbaryl 
CropLife America (CLA) represents the developers, manufacturers, formulators, and distributors of 
pesticides for agriculture and pest management in the United States. As such, we are uniquely positioned 
to assist the Environmental Protection Agency (the EPA or the Agency) in their efforts to implement an 
enhanced pesticide registration review process in keeping with the EPA work plan released April 12, 
2022. Carbaryl is one of the first pesticides to move through the enhanced registration review process. 
The EPA released the proposed interim registration review decision (PID) for carbaryl on December 1, 
2022 for public comment. This report contains CLA’s comments on this PID for carbaryl, but many of the 
comments are also likely to apply to future pesticide registration decisions.  
CLA would like to recognize that the EPA worked with multiple stakeholders during the development of 
the PID. CLA and its member companies look forward to continuing and expanding opportunities for 
collaboration with the EPA and other regulatory authorities (e.g., the Fish and Wildlife Service (FWS) and 
National Marine Fisheries Service (NMFS) (the Services collectively)), to achieve a registration review 
program that provides predictable, scientifically defensible, and consistent results for all stakeholders 
while also providing statutory protection for listed species.  
The main issues we identified with the PID include the timing and lack of scientific basis for some of the 
mitigations being proposed. As the Agency is aware, the Services have been working for some time on 
the EPA-requested consultations for carbaryl, with draft biological opinions (BiOps) expected from both 
Services this year. We are concerned with how EPA will reconcile mitigations identified in this PID and 
mitigations that may be proposed once the BiOps are complete. EPA states that they will complete 
consultation with the Services prior to completing the carbaryl registration in the PID.  As such, it is 
unclear why mitigations are being proposed at this juncture. It would be far more efficient and less 
confusing to growers, registrants, and others if changes to carbaryl labels were implemented once during 
the registration review process. 
There is limited scientific justification for proposed mitigations. Some of the runoff mitigations proposed by 
the EPA have not been clearly defined and none of them are clearly linked to the population-level 
protection goals of the Endangered Species Act (ESA). There should be appropriate methods (e.g., 
population modeling) and best available data applied to support the recommended mitigations.  
We hope that the comments provided here will assist the EPA and the Services in moving towards an 
efficient and scientifically-defensible process that is protective of the environment and which provides 
certainty in the regulatory process for our members, pesticide users, and other stakeholders.

INTRODUCTION 
To account for evolving science and methodologies which can change the understanding of pesticide 
use, carbaryl is currently undergoing registration review and EPA has released the PID for public 
comment (EPA, 2022a). CLA has reviewed the carbaryl PID and provides the following comments. Our 
focus is on policy and technical considerations, and our comments are directed at improving the carbaryl 
PID and subsequent Interim Decision or Final Decision.   
POLICY CONSIDERATIONS FOR THE AGENCY 
Stakeholder Engagement 
Stakeholder engagement is a key requirement of the registration review process, particularly with the 
addition of the endangered species component to the PID (EPA, 2022a). Stakeholders, including 
registrants and growers familiar with carbaryl, can provide EPA with much-needed context and expertise 
during the registration review process, including through comments posted to the docket. Registrants 
have broad information about their products, can often provide best available data for registration review, 
and can potentially provide expertise and knowledge on product use and other information that may be 
important to EPA evaluations and the development of mitigations. In the case of carbaryl, EPA has 
discussed upfront mitigations and consideration for four listed species: Upper Columbia River steelhead 
trout, Miami tiger beetle, wireweed, and Squirrel Chimney cave shrimp. CLA looks forward to continuing 
and expanding opportunities for collaboration with EPA, the Services, the US Department of Agriculture 
(USDA), and other stakeholders to achieve a registration review program that provides predictable, 
scientifically defensible, and consistent results for all stakeholders while also protecting listed and other 
non-target species. 
TECHNICAL CONSIDERATIONS 
Approach and Methodology 
CLA recognizes the work that the Agency has accomplished during the registration review process for 
carbaryl. In this instance there is increased complexity due to the developing approach to endangered 
species risk assessment and associated  proposed mitigations and label language. With respect to the 
listed species portion of the PID (EPA, 2022a), the Agency has moved in a positive direction relative to 
some of the early biological evaluations (BEs). Additionally, EPA has applied experience gained from the 
FWS biological opinion for malathion. Examples of these improvements include applying more species-
specific information (e.g., dietary, habitat requirements), accounting for existing management areas and 
localized management plans, considering wind direction and likelihood of intercept from physical

Mitigations

Carbaryl registrants proposed a suite of changes to the carbaryl labels to mitigate exposure to listed

Please accept the following comments from the Center for Biological Diversity (“Center”) in 
response to the Environmental Protection Agency’s (“EPA”) Proposed Interim Decision for 
carbaryl. 
 
The Center is a non-profit environmental organization dedicated to the protection of native 
species and their habitats through science, policy, and environmental law. The Center has over 
1.7 million members and online activists dedicated to the protection and restoration of 
endangered species and wild places. The Center has worked for thirty-three years to protect 
imperiled plants and wildlife, open space, air and water quality, and overall quality of life. The 
Center’s Environmental Health Program aims to secure programmatic changes in the pesticide 
registration process including securing the completion and implementation of ESA consultations 
for all pesticides in order to ensure that the nation’s most imperiled species have a fighting 
chance in their battle against extinction.  
 
We appreciate the opportunity to provide comment. 
 
The Proposed Interim Decision (“PID”) for carbaryl presents some broad changes to the carbaryl 
label and mitigations meant to establish minimum mitigations (in the form of Bulletins) for four 
at-risk ESA-listed pilot species. The broad label changes and mitigations for the pilot species are 
a step in the right direction, but we remain concerned that label language and proposed 
mitigations remain insufficiently protective and are not targeted enough to make the Bulletins 
Live II (“BLT”) approach meaningful on the ground. 
 
It is absolutely essential that EPA use the pilot species mitigation project to put in place strong, 
efficient, targeted mitigations that can be replicated to other ESA-listed species as part of its 
ongoing consultation with the Services. Below we outline ways that this pilot process can 
achieve adequate protections for the vulnerable plants and animals protected under the ESA. We 
also outline our strong disagreement with EPA’s attempt to offer alternative Reasonable and 

Prudent Alternatives (“RPAs”) in relation to the National Marine Fisheries Service (“NMFS”) 
completed 2009 carbaryl biological opinion (“BiOp”).     
 
In short, our comments include the following positions: 
 
1) Carbaryl use should be prohibited in designated critical habitat of all listed species 
throughout the entire year, excepting for pesticide use that directly benefits a listed 
species or a legitimate conservation or human health objective, such as removing 
invasive species or treating serious disease.  
2) To address runoff in an enforceable and implementable manner, EPA should implement a 
standard, minimum 100 ft buffer from waterways to protect listed species. A 25-foot 
buffer is simply too small, too easy for non-compliant entities to ignore, and too difficult 
to enforce. Included together with the standard 100-foot buffer, EPA should also require 
a standard, minimum 30-foot vegetative filter strip. 
3) To address drift and/or volatilization, EPA should implement a standard, minimum 100-
foot omnidirectional buffer for ground applications and aerial application should not be 
allowed for any use. If aerial application is allowed, it should have at least a 250-foot 
omnidirectional buffer for aerial applications to protect listed species. Wind-direction 
contingent buffers are not effective, not enforceable, and provide a massive loophole 
(e.g., any person can claim wind was not blowing when spraying occurred) that makes 
such mitigation essentially useless. 
4) While such standard, minimum buffers for runoff, drift and/or volatilization should be 
required on all labels, EPA should clarify and make clear to registrants that such 
measures are the minimum additional label changes for Bulletins Live II. A menu of 
additional mitigation options may still be required to both avoid jeopardy, and crucially, 
minimize avoidable take as the Endangered Species Act requires.  
5) Together with stronger, more enforceable mitigations, Bulletins must have far greater 
specificity to areas where species presently occur. Such information generally exists and 
our comments discuss this in detail below.  
6) Any effort to minimize avoidable take should include tank mix restrictions in the form of 
requiring rate reductions when pesticides that affect the same organ system are mixed.  
7) It is unnecessary, and contrary to the plain language, law and spirit of the ESA, to 
conduct a cost-benefit analysis – especially for Bulletin mitigations.     
8) The many legal and scientific flaws of the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (“FWS”) 
malathion BiOp must preclude its use as a blueprint for making predictive jeopardy 
determinations. The NMFS malathion BiOp provides a far superior blueprint both legally 
and scientifically. 
 
 
 

I. 
EPA Predictive Jeopardy Approach to Endangered Species Act Compliance 
 
It is important to recognize several critical limitations with the EPA’s approach in assessing the 
likely harms to listed species. First and foremost, the EPA does not possess the statutory 
authority or scientific expertise to correctly assess or make “predictive” determinations regarding 
jeopardy to any listed species, as such determinations can only be made by the U.S. Fish and 
Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service during formal consultations under the 
Endangered Species Act. Jeopardy can only be assessed in context of the full suite of threats to 
any given species, after considerations of the environmental baseline, cumulative effects and the 
real-world conservation status of any given species, none of which are considered by the EPA in 
its Proposed Interim Decision. However, we recognize that the EPA is making efforts to make 
strides in protecting species from pesticides and commend its efforts.  
 
We do agree that the EPA can, somewhat accurately, assess the relative likelihood of severe 
harm to listed species from pesticides, but its methodologies continue to overlook key 
information including, for example, the relative extinction risk within taxonomic groups of 
similar species. Thus, while the Center does not necessarily fault the selection of the four pilot 
species here, we note that other species may have presented better opportunities to put in place 
conservation measures for even-more imperiled species than the ones selected. 
 
Second, it is vital for the EPA to recognize that the consultation process contains two, mandatory 
statutory goals: (1) avoiding jeopardy or adverse modification of critical habitat, and (2) 
minimization of unavoidable take in situations where jeopardy will not occur.1 To the extent that 
EPA’s Proposed Interim Decision might mean that the registration of carbaryl will avoid 
jeopardy for a subset of listed species, that is certainly positive. However, reducing take to a 
level that possibly avoids jeopardy does not mean that EPA has satisfied the requirements of the 
ESA, all unavoidable take must be minimized in order to receive an Incidental Take Statement. 
The Center supports the EPA’s efforts to reduce take to listed species at the front-end of 
consultation and at every opportunity during EPA’s registration review processes, but it should 
not, and may not legally, create the expectation that these initial mitigation measures are 
sufficient for full compliance with the Endangered Species Act. 
 
Finally, we would also like to emphasize that the EPA’s over-reliance on the conclusions within 
the FWS’s malathion BiOp is extraordinarily problematic. The BiOp remains fatally flawed and 
would not withstand judicial review, in part because it failed to fully assess the full range of 
harms from insecticides for many listed species, and both its draft and final conclusions 
regarding jeopardy are highly problematic. Excessive reliance by the EPA on the FWS BiOp will

cause the EPA problems down the road. We urge the EPA to look to the NMFS chlorpyrifos,

II. 
General Label Changes and Mitigation Measures 
While the pilot species are clearly vulnerable to carbaryl, we would like to note that many other 
listed species that may or may not be less highly exposed or at risk than these three pilot species 
are still likely to be jeopardized by EPA’s action. It is equally clear that many more species 
deserve similar protections from harm by this dangerous pesticide. This exercise does not excuse 
EPA from its duties to these other species. 
Usage data are not the best available science for determining a pesticide use footprint because 
they are not transparent, reliable or accurately predictive of future use – especially in this era of 
climate chaos. Reliance on usage data limits the accuracy of the EPA’s conclusions regarding 
likely harm to listed species from carbaryl. 
Of utmost importance when designing label mitigations is that they are effective, simple, likely 
to be followed and enforceable. None of the proposed Bulletin mitigations achieve these four 
requirements. Prohibitions on applying pesticides when the wind is blowing in a certain direction 
or when it may or may not rain in an amount that will produce runoff in the next two days is 
insufficient for several reasons. These requirements are rife with subjectivity and are in many 
ways unenforceable. Mitigations that have a clear potential to be violated will not achieve their 
intended purpose and do not meet the legal standards required by the Endangered Species Act. 
Below we propose mitigations that are strong and simple in an effort to strengthen compliance 
and protect species.  
A) Critical Habitat Must be Fully Protected from Pesticides 
All pesticide use should cease in designated critical habitat of all listed species throughout the 
entire year, excepting any use that directly benefits a listed species or a legitimate conservation

D) Inadequate Protections from Pesticide Runoff 
Carbaryl presents considerable risk of runoff, and the label needs to require substantial runoff 
mitigations even after proposed use deletions and rate reductions. Carbaryl is mobile, does not 
appreciably bind to soil (Koc=153), and has an aerobic soil half-life of 4-253 days depending on 
the soil and other factors.7 The PID presents several mitigations meant to reduce runoff in urban 
areas, but presents inadequate, boilerplate mitigations across all labels.  
EPA proposed three broad label changes to address runoff restricting application if there is rain 
forecast within 48-hours, when it is raining, and when the soil is saturated.8 These runoff 
mitigations are woefully insufficient for several reasons including enforceability and vagueness. 
EPA has provided no evidence that a prohibition on applying a pesticide with the chemical 
characteristics of carbaryl within 48 hours of heavy rain will appreciably reduce runoff 
concentrations. A prohibition on applying the pesticide within two days of major rainfall may 
slightly reduce the amount of pesticide available for runoff, but it certainly will not appreciably 
lower concentrations. Carbaryl’s average half-life is greater than 100-days and a two day period 
before rain will not result in any meaningful breakdown. Even assuming a 4-day half-life, 50% 
of the applied carbaryl would remain and when it rains or the field is irrigated, nearly all the 
applied carbaryl could partition with the water and runoff into streams. Additionally, prohibiting 
spraying when it is “likely to produce runoff” is entirely subjective. Enforcement of the EPA’s

Drift and volatilization present serious, widespread threats to ESA-listed and non-listed wildlife.

complied with and are impossible to enforce. A recent survey of farmers in Missouri indicated 
that less than half – only 43 percent – actually read the label each time they use pesticides.12 Four

Restrictions on tank mixing and certain multi-ingredient pesticides in listed species habitat must 
become a common fixture in developing mitigations to prevent jeopardy and adverse 
modification and minimizing avoidable take. We understand that this is an area EPA habitually 
avoids, perhaps because it is a complicated arena to wade into, but the allowance of these 
mixtures is an unavoidable part of the action EPA is taking and therefore must be mitigated.  
A template for how this could look is contained in NMFS’s past BiOps. Specifically, in the 
chlorpyrifos, diazinon and malathion BiOps, NMFS required a prohibition on applying those

IV. 
Cost-Benefit Balancing for the Proposed Pilot Mitigations is Unlawful  
We fully understand the complexities involved in implementing ESA-specific mitigations in the 
context of a preliminary interim decision, which is a FIFRA action. The EPA typically conducts 
a cost-benefit balancing for its FIFRA actions, while the ESA specifically forbids it. 
In EPA’s recent ESA workplan update,37 it appears that EPA intends to do a cost-benefit 
balancing when it proposes broad label mitigations. The agency views these actions as furthering 
its FIFRA obligations because these mitigations have broad ecological benefits, not just to listed 
species.38 However, EPA also believes that targeted mitigations to protect certain listed species, 
in the form of Bulletins or certain geographies, do not require a cost-benefit balancing because 
that action is governed by the ESA standard.39 Importantly, EPA states that this is also the case 
when the targeted mitigation is included through registration review.  
The carbaryl PID proposes several broad label changes that impact applicator safety and other 
changes relevant to non-listed species that would be subject to a FIFRA-style cost-benefit 
balancing. However, we are perplexed at the existence of multiple BEAD documents40 that 
assess the impacts of both broad label changes and ESA-specific mitigations. The purpose of 
these benefits documents was—among other things—to detail the benefits that carbaryl offers 
farmers and the costs they would incur by complying with the proposed mitigations, including 
those intended to address J/AM and take to ESA-listed species.  
We understand that the Services do not have completed BiOps for this pesticide or likely for 
future pesticides, so EPA has no clear mandate for how to mitigate harms to ESA-listed species. 
In the absence of a completed BiOp, ESA has chosen to develop its own proposed mitigations. 
However, preventing jeopardy/adverse modification and minimizing incidental take are still all 
that should be considered when proposing mitigations in this, and future, ESA analyses.  
Conducting a cost-benefit analysis of species-specific mitigations in this pilot or any future 
proposed species mitigation is unlawful, undermines the ESA and is in direct violation of EPA’s 
recent workplan update.41 EPA cannot use a cost-benefit analysis to determine the details of 
mitigations required to avoid jeopardy/adverse modification and minimize any incidental take in 
their proposed mitigations or when required in Service BiOps. In this and in future pesticide

VII. 
Conclusions 
We generally support EPA’s recognition that compliance with the Endangered Species Act will 
require several strategies, some of which will overlap. Such mitigations can be achieved through 
broad label changes, either those that encompass the entire U.S., state-level strategies in places 
like Hawaii, strategies that focus on high pesticide use areas that have a high concentration of at-
risk species (like CA’s Central Valley or FL’s Lake Wales Ridge), and geographically targeted 
Bulletins that provide specific conservation measures for species that require unique protections 
from pesticides. 
We again wish to raise our concerns with the EPA’s overreliance on the fundamentally flawed 
FWS malathion BiOp as its guide for predicting jeopardy and adverse modification. The NMFS 
chlorpyrifos, diazinon and malathion BiOps (as well as many of the regional BiOps completed 
by NMFS) provide a much more scientifically and legally-sound way of predicting jeopardy and 
adverse modification and should be the sole methodology used by the EPA moving forward. 
Bulletins must be targeted, detailed and clear to be protective, enforceable, and implemented. 
The three Bulletins proposed here fall short of these requirements. We strongly encourage the 
EPA to reach out more proactively to stakeholders and dive into the weeds of the species in far 
greater detail than just a species’ range or critical habitat and develop strategies to move beyond 
superficial narrative descriptions of a species’ habitat needs.  
EPA must significantly bolster its proposed mitigations. The current mitigations proposed in 
these pilot Bulletins are overly subjective, will be plagued by a lack of compliance and are 
completely unenforceable. We have proposed simple, straightforward buffer language that can 
be easily understood, implemented and will be protective of listed species. 
Additionally, we must start seeing proposed restrictions on co-applying pesticides in species’ 
habitat to prevent jeopardy and adverse modification and minimize incidental take. EPA cannot 
ignore the potential impacts of pesticide mixtures. NMFS has proposed a reasonable way 

forward with requiring reduced application rates for co-applied pesticides in all listed species’ 
habitat. We support this proposed path forward and urge EPA to finally confront this issue. 
EPA must explicitly communicate its position on cost-benefit balancing as the agency begins to 
come into compliance with the ESA. This is incredibly important, as the agency is fully aware 
that the ESA specifically forbids such an analysis. From our perspective, it is clear that EPA has 
already violated its stated policy in the ESA workplan to not account for the perceived impacts to 
agriculture in ESA-specific actions by doing just that in the targeted mitigations proposed here. 
Clarification is needed. 
Finally, EPA’s proposed alternative RPAs for the 2009 NMFS carbaryl BiOp are unacceptable 
and contradict how NMFS has designed RPAs in recent BiOps. The proposed alternatives are 
considerably weaker than those required by NMFS in 2009 and are in no way sufficient to 
prevent jeopardy.

III. UC Pest Management Guidelines: Tadpole Shrimp 
“Scientific name: Triops longicaudatus 
Common name: Tadpole Shrimp 
DESCRIPTION OF THE PESTS 
Although they are crustaceans, tadpole shrimp resemble tadpoles in size, shape, color, and 
mobility. Tadpole shrimp have about 35 body segments, and all but the last six or seven have 
pairs of leaflike, gill-bearing appendages. A thin, olive-brown shield covers the front section 
of the body, and two long tails extend from the last segment. Two long, jointed appendages 
resembling antennae extend from below the well-developed chewing mandibles. 
Adults deposit eggs singly on soil or on plants at the bottom of the field. They are highly 
resistant to drying and remain viable for several years in unflooded soil. Most of the eggs 
hatch 1 to 3 days after spring flooding of the rice fields, but hatching may continue for 1 to 2 
weeks. The young develop rapidly by a series of molts and resemble the adults in less than 
24 hours. They feed on a variety of small animals and plants commensurate with their size 
as they grow and molt. The somewhat transparent molt skins may be mistaken for dead 
shrimp. The first instar larva is about 0.2 inch (5 mm) long. Egg pouches are first noted 
when shrimp are about 0.63 inch (16 mm) long, and by 3 weeks old the shrimp may be 1 
inch (2.5 cm) long. At maturity, tadpole shrimp are about 1.5 inches long. Masses of red-
orange eggs occur in 7 to 10 days from hatching in two brood pouches on the appendages of 
the 11th segment at the lower margin of the shield. 
DAMAGE 
Tadpole shrimp cause losses in seedling rice stands in two ways. First, they may chew off the 
coleoptile, roots, and leaves of the seedling, and uproot seedlings with their digging and 
feeding activity, all of which may kill the plants. Second, their digging activities associated 
with egg laying muddy the water, reducing light penetration and thereby slow the growth of 
the submerged seedlings. Tadpole shrimp cause no injury to rice once leaves have reached 
the water surface and roots are well established in the soil.

MANAGEMENT 
Management of tadpole shrimp involves rapid seeding of the field after flooding and 
monitoring twice within the first 2 weeks following flooding to determine the need for 
chemical treatment. As an alternative, some population reduction can be obtained by 
flooding and draining the field before flooding for seeding. 
 
Cultural Control 
 
Most tadpole shrimp eggs hatch within 2 days after contact with water. The longer the time 
between hatching of the eggs and planting, the larger the size of the shrimp and the greater 
the potential for plant injury. Flood the field as fast as possible, and seed as soon as possible 
after flooding has been initiated. In very large fields that take more than a few days to flood, 
you may want to seed basins (checks) in sequence as they fill with water. Rice stands that 
have been reduced by shrimp feeding can be reseeded but generally a good stand of rice is 
difficult to establish in this manner. 
 
Flooding and draining the field before planting will kill hatched tadpole shrimp through 
desiccation and are alternatives to chemical control. Do not drain the field until 4 to 5 days 
after initial flood so the maximum egg hatch can occur. The draining time will vary based on 
soil type and weather but should continue for at least 24 hours after all standing water is 
gone. Shrimp will gather in standing water in low areas and will reinfest the field if the drain 
period is too short. Reflooding may result in some shrimp from previously unhatched eggs, 
but they would be in noneconomic numbers and less likely to damage the older, firmer 
rooted seedlings. Any soil cultivation following the drain period may bring viable, unhatched 
shrimp eggs to the soil surface for possible infestation upon reflooding, however. 
 
A decision to drain must take into account possible negative aspects such as fertilizer loss, 
encouragement of weeds, or interruption of weed control procedures, interruption of 
pesticide holding requirements, and the economics of irrigation. 
 
Organically Acceptable Methods 
 
Draining, as described under cultural controls, and applications of copper sulfate are 
organically acceptable methods. 
 
Monitoring 
 
Check all your fields during seedling development, but give special attention to those that 
had significant populations of tadpole shrimp last year. Even though infestations may have 
been localized in previous years, monitor all quadrants of the field because the shrimp can 
occur well beyond previously observed boundaries. Masses of wind-blown cut leaves and 
floating seedlings along the levees combined with muddy water are good evidence of

The action threshold is determined by counting numbers of seedlings at various stages of 
development. Take samples twice during seedling development: at 5 to 7 days after flooding

open ends that encloses 1 square foot and with sides higher than the water depth, to count

push it down into the cloudy water until you can see the bottom of the field and move the jar 
around to see the seedlings. Take 10 samples across the check on each sampling date. Take 
20 samples if your checks are large. The treatment guidelines below are based on a seeding 
rate of 150 pound per acre. 
 
Treatment Decisions 
 
Take the first sample 5 to 7 days after flooding begins. Treat if tadpole shrimp or their 
molted skins are present and less than 30 healthy seedlings per square foot are found, and 
there is damage due to shrimp feeding. 
 
Take the second sample 8 to 14 days after flooding. An average of 25 or more healthy 
seedlings per square foot at this time should provide a good stand. Treat if less than 25 
healthy seedlings are found and evidence of shrimp is present in the monitoring area. If 25 
or more healthy seedlings are found but there is also evidence of tadpole shrimp activity, 
repeat the sampling procedure every 2 to 3 days until rice plants emerge above the water 
surface. Treat if the average number of seedlings drops below 25 plants. 
 
If muddy water does not allow an adequate visual inspection of the plant stand after 8 days, 
treatment decisions must be based on the presence of shrimp and shed skins, and 
observations of chewed shoot tips or roots, or uprooted floating seedlings.

IV. Cultural Practices 
 
In the Central Valley north of Sacramento, the majority of rice is grown on clay soil primarily 
unsuitable for supporting other crops (CH2M Hill 1992.) Therefore, crop rotation is not 
common on rice ground. Approximately 98 to 99 percent of California rice is seeded in 
standing water at three to five inches deep. The field preparation and rice planting are 
weather dependent. Weather can delay the planting process, but there never is a time when 
the season starts early due to unusually dry conditions as the temperatures are too cool for 
germination, and the early planted rice becomes feed for late migrating waterfowl. 
 
 
 
A. Field preparation 
 
Water can be held on the harvested (non-crop period) rice fields over the winter months 
with draining starting at the end of February, first of March. The harvested fields usually fill 
from rainfall. These wet fields facilitate the decomposition of the stubble remaining after 
harvest. The winter flooded fields provide habitat for migration waterfowl along the Pacific 
Flyway.

Food to sustain the waterfowl comes from spent grain left from the harvester, and insects 
living in the mud. With the loss in wetlands for flood control, the rice fields provide 300,000 
acres of winter habitat. Considerable research in collaboration with the industry, the 
Universities, and several avian groups demonstrate the benefits rice fields provide to 
wildlife. Section V cites some of the decades of work and studies on impacts to waterfowl.  
 
After the field is drained, the soil is disked to open up the top layer allowing it to aerate. 
Additional equipment is used to break-up the disked soil into a finer, smoother texture. 
Preplant fertilizer is incorporated at this time. The fields are leveled to slopes of 0.05 to 0.1 
percent to allow for drainage. A grooved roller is pulled over the leveled field to create small 
rolls of ridges (UCCE/UCANR, Land Formation 2015).  
 
Water is then added to the field at a depth of three to five inches. The rice seed is soaked in 
water 24 to 48 hours before planting. Soaking the seed starts the germination process and 
adds weight. The soaked seed is flown onto the field dropping through the water and settling 
into a groove formed during field preparation.  
 
Seedlings will break through the water and remain vulnerable to insect infestation, or 
dislodging until the plant tillers and begins forming the canopy. Once the rice stand is 
established, the plant is naturally resistant to insect infestation under normal conditions 
(UCCE/UCANR 2015, Planting & Stand Establishment).

B. Rice seeding 
 
Approximately one to two percent of California rice is dry seeded. Dry seeding helps to 
break up the weed cycle due to the limited number of available herbicides with differing 
modes of action.

Water seeding became an industry wide practice around 1982 (Div. of Ag. Sci. 1982). The 
initial rational was to allow the pre-germinated seed an opportunity to break the water 
surface in advance of the weeds for non-chemical control. In addition to weed control, water 
seeding facilitates nitrogen nutrition and increases productivity. The rice seed is water 
soaked 24 to 48 hours in large bins that are drained before the seed is transferred to trucks 
and delivered to the fields. The seed is transferred from the truck to an airplane and flown 
onto the prepared, flooded field. 
 
The water is kept on the field throughout the season except for short-term drainage, 
permanently removing it only at the end of the growing season to prepare the crop for 
harvest. Water depth is maintained at three to five inches for three or more months 
depending on the pest pressure to the crop.  
 
As previously stated, California rice is most susceptible to damage during the first six weeks 
after seeding, the time it takes for the crop to set roots and break through the water. 
Growers refer to this critical time as stand establishment when the plants are most 
vulnerable to insect pressure (UCCE/UCANR 2015, Planting & Stand Establishment; 
UCCE/UCANR 2015, Water Management). 
 
Whether rice growers water or dry seed, the water is added and cultural practices are 
identical for the growing season. The flooding of rice fields during the production stage 
involves the same practices whether the crop was dry, or water seeded.  
 
The number of plants per square foot can vary from 12 to 46 (UCCE/UCANR 2015, Planting 
and Stand Establishment). Minimum seedling population for maximum yield is dependent 
on many factors including sowing method, water management, planting date, rice variety 
and soil type (UCCE/UCANR 2015, Planting & Stand Establishment).

VI. Summary 
 
The CRC realizes that carbaryl usage has declined significantly on rice. However, carbaryl is 
one of the few tools registered for tadpole shrimp control, a significant seedling pest. Our 
comments intend to define the need for carbaryl, while addressing potential questions and 
concerns from the use of insecticides on California rice.  
 
Water holding requirements can be a form of mitigation. However, the insecticides typically 
have a water hold duration of seven to 14 days. It is critical the water holding requirements 
are not extensive for early season insecticides. Several of the herbicides require a water 
draw down prior to application because lower in field water allows for contact to the weed. 
Any removal of water during a water hold is a violation, and the reason for a need of shorter 
durations in days for the insecticides.   
We value our positive relationship with staff at the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency. 
Our comments provide additional clarity in the overall assessment of rice while justifying 
the need for carbaryl as a minor use product to this important California crop. Please contact 
us for further information and clarification of our comments.
